text:
The following are contained in the fifteenth of the books of Diodorus.
How the Persians waged the war against Evagoras in Cyprus.
How the Lacedaemonians, contrary to the common agreements, removed the Mantineans from their fatherland.
Concerning the poems of Dionysius the tyrant.
Concerning the arrest of Tiribazus and his acquittal.
Concerning the death of Glos and the condemnation of Orontes.
How Amyntas and the Lacedaemonians made war upon the Olynthians.
How the Lacedaemonians seized the Cadmeia.
How they enslaved the Greek cities contrary to the treaties.
The founding of the island Pharos in the Adriatic.
The expedition of Dionysius into Tyrrhenia and the plundering of the temple.
The expedition of Dionysius against the Carthaginians, and a victory and a defeat.
How the Thebans recovered the Cadmeia.
How the Carthaginians, falling into a pestilential disease, were endangered.
Concerning the Boeotian War and what was done in it.
The expedition of the Triballi against Abdera.
The expedition of the Persians against Egypt.
How the Thebans, having conquered the Lacedaemonians in a most notable battle at Leuctra, laid claim to the leadership of the Greeks.
What was done by the Thebans in their invasions of the Peloponnese.
Concerning the training of Iphicrates and the things invented by him for campaigns.
The expedition of the Lacedaemonians against Corcyra.
Concerning the earthquake and flood that occurred about the Peloponnese, and the torch that appeared in the heavens.
How among the Argives there occurred a great slaughter called the clubbing.
Concerning Jason the tyrant of Pherae and his successors.
The resettlement of Messene by the Thebans.
The expedition of the Boeotians into Thessaly.

1.1. Throughout the whole work being accustomed to use the frankness usual to history, and to add the just praise to good men upon their noble deeds, and to deem the base, when they do wrong, worthy of just censure, we think that by such a method we shall both incite those well disposed by nature toward virtue, through the immortality conferred by glory, to undertake the noblest deeds, and shall turn away those of the contrary disposition, by the fitting reproaches, from their impulse toward wickedness.
1.2. Therefore, being come in our writing to those times in which the Lacedaemonians, unexpectedly defeated at Leuctra, fell into a great calamity, and again, stumbling at Mantinea, lost beyond hope the leadership of the Greeks, we think it our duty to preserve the principle of our writing and to make the fitting censure of the Lacedaemonians.
1.3. For who would not consider them worthy of accusation, who, having received from their forefathers a leadership most nobly founded, and preserved through the virtue of their ancestors for more than five hundred years, then looked on while it was dissolved through their own folly—not unreasonably? For those who had lived before them had acquired by many toils and great dangers so great a glory, dealing fairly and humanely with their subjects; but the later generations, dealing violently and harshly with their allies, and besides constituting unjust and arrogant wars against the Greeks, not unreasonably lost their rule through their own follies.
1.4. For in their misfortunes the hatred of the wronged found an opportunity to take vengeance on those who had wronged them first, and upon men who from their forefathers had been unconquered there followed so great a contempt as is likely to arise against those who destroy the virtues of their forefathers.
1.5. Therefore the Thebans, who before for many generations had been subject to their betters, then unexpectedly conquering these became leaders of the Greeks, while the Lacedaemonians, after the loss of their leadership, were never able to recover the dignity of their ancestors.
1.6. Having censured them sufficiently, we shall pass to the continuous narrative of our history, after first defining the times proper to the writing. The book before this, being the fourteenth of the whole work, ended its events at the enslavement of the Rhegians by Dionysius and the capture of Rome by the Gauls, which occurred in the year before the expedition of the Persians into Cyprus against King Evagoras; in this book, beginning from this war, we shall end at the year before the kingship of Philip the son of Amyntas.
2.1. For in the archonship at Athens of Mystichides the Romans appointed three military tribunes in place of the consuls, Marcus Furius, and besides Gaius and Aemilius. In this year Artaxerxes the King of the Persians campaigned against Evagoras the king of Cyprus. Having for a long time been occupied with the preparations for the war, he assembled a great force both naval and infantry; for the infantry army was thirty myriads with the cavalry, and he constructed more than three hundred triremes.
2.2. He appointed as generals of the infantry force Orontes his son-in-law, and of the naval force Tiribazus, a man enjoying great esteem among the Persians. These, taking over the forces at Phocaea and Cyme, came to Cilicia, and crossing over to Cyprus carried on the war vigorously.
2.3. Evagoras made an alliance with Acoris the king of the Egyptians, who was an enemy of the Persians, and obtained from him a considerable force; and from Hecatomnus the ruler of Caria, who secretly cooperated with him, he received a quantity of money for the maintenance of foreign forces; likewise too the others who were ill disposed toward the Persians, some secretly, some openly, he drew into sharing in the Persian war.
2.4. He was master in Cyprus of almost all the cities, and in Phoenicia of Tyre and certain others. He had ninety triremes, of which twenty were Tyrian and seventy Cyprian, and of his own soldiers six thousand, and from the allies far more than these. Besides these he enlisted many mercenaries, having abundance of money. The king of the Arabs also sent him not a few soldiers, and certain others who were under suspicion with the King of the Persians.
3.1. He, then, having so great resources, went down confidently to the war. And first, having not a few piratical ships, he lay in wait for the provisions of the enemy as they were conveyed, and some of them he destroyed at sea, others he prevented, and some he carried off. Therefore, the merchants not daring to convey grain to Cyprus, and great forces being gathered on the island, a famine quickly held the camp of the Persians.
3.2. The scarcity leading to faction, the mercenaries of the Persians, rushing upon the commanders and slaying some, filled the camp with tumult and faction. Hardly did the generals of the Persians and the leader of the naval force, named Glos, put an end to the faction.
3.3. Sailing out with the whole fleet and conveying a quantity of grain from Cilicia, they provided much abundance of food. To Evagoras a sufficient quantity of grain King Acoris conveyed from Egypt, and money and the rest of a sufficient supply he sent out.
3.4. Evagoras, seeing himself far inferior in naval force, manned sixty other ships and sent for fifty from Acoris out of Egypt, so as to have in all two hundred triremes. Adorning these strikingly for a sea-battle, and making continual trials and exercises, he prepared for a sea-fight. Therefore, when the royal fleet was sailing along to Citium, attacking the ships unexpectedly, he had many advantages over the Persians.
3.5. For he attacked with ships drawn up in order against ships in disorder, and fighting with men forewarned against men unprepared, he immediately at the first encounter prepared the victory beforehand; for, attacking with his triremes in close order against ships scattered and in confusion, some he destroyed, others he mastered.
3.6. Nevertheless, the admiral of the Persians, Glos, and the other commanders withstanding nobly, a fierce sea-battle took place, in which Evagoras at first had the advantage, but afterward, Glos bearing on with weight and fighting nobly, it came to pass that the men of Evagoras fled and lost many of their triremes.
4.1. The Persians, victorious in the sea-battle, gathered both forces at the city Citium. Setting out from this, they constituted a siege against Salamis, and ravaged the city both by land and by sea.
4.2. Tiribazus, after the sea-battle, crossing to Cilicia and going from there to the King, both reported the victory and brought back two thousand talents for the war; while Evagoras, before the sea-battle, having engaged on land by the sea with a part of the infantry force, had had the advantage and become confident for the future, but, having stumbled in the sea-battle and being shut up in a siege, was despondent.
4.3. Nevertheless, deciding to hold to the war, he left his son Pnytagoras, making him leader of all affairs in Cyprus, while he himself, taking ten triremes, by night unobserved by the enemy sailed out of Salamis. Conveyed to Egypt and meeting the king, he urged him to hold firmly to the war and to consider the war against the Persians a common one.

5.1. At the same time as these things were being done, the Lacedaemonians resolved to campaign against Mantinea, taking no thought of the treaties that had been made, for the following causes. There being already among the Greeks the common peace of Antalcidas, by which all the cities had got rid of their garrisons and received their independence by agreement, the Lacedaemonians, being by nature lovers of rule and warlike in their inclinations, did not endure the peace as a heavy burden, and longing for the dominion of Greece they had formerly held, were excited in their impulses toward revolution.
5.2. Immediately, then, they threw the cities into disorder and through their own friends contrived factions in them, of which some furnished plausible occasions to them for the disturbance. For having recovered their independence, they demanded an account from those who had presided over them during the leadership of the Lacedaemonians; and the reckonings being bitter because the peoples bore malice, and many being banished, they declared themselves helpers of those who were being put down by faction.
5.3. Receiving these and sending them out with a force for their returns, they enslaved first the weaker cities, and after this subduing the more notable ones too they made them subject, not even keeping the common treaties two years. Seeing that the city of the Mantineans was a neighbour and full of valiant men, they suspected its increase that came from the peace, and were eager to humble the spirits of the men.
5.4. Therefore at first, sending envoys to Mantinea, they ordered them to tear down their walls and themselves to remove, all of them, into the ancient five villages, out of which they had originally united into Mantinea. No one heeding them, they sent out a force and besieged the city.
5.5. The Mantineans, sending envoys to Athens, asked them to help them. The Athenians not choosing to transgress the common treaties, nevertheless by themselves the Mantineans, withstanding the siege, vigorously defended themselves against the enemy. And the affairs of Greece in this manner took the beginning of new wars.
6.1. In Sicily Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans, being released from the wars against the Carthaginians, had much peace and leisure. Therefore he undertook to write poems with much eagerness, and he sent for those who had a reputation in these, and honouring them above others he spent his time with them and had them as overseers and correctors of his poems. Being lifted up by these, because of his benefactions, with flattering speeches, he boasted much more over his poems than over his successes in war.
6.2. Of the poets who were with him, Philoxenus the dithyrambic poet, who had the greatest reputation for the composition of his own poetry, at the symposium, when the poems of the tyrant, being wretched, had been read, was asked what judgement he had concerning the poems. He answering rather frankly, the tyrant, taking offence at what was said, and blaming him that out of envy he had spoken slander, ordered the servants at once to lead him off to the quarries.
6.3. On the next day, the friends urging him to give pardon to Philoxenus, being reconciled with him he again took the same men to the symposium. As the drinking advanced, and again Dionysius boasted about his own poems, and brought forward certain verses of those that seemed successful, and asked, "What sort do the poems appear to you to be?"—he said nothing else, but calling the servants of Dionysius, ordered them to lead him off to the quarries.
6.4. At that time, then, on account of the wit of his words, Dionysius, smiling, bore the frankness, the laughter blunting the censure; but a little later, when both his acquaintances and Dionysius were deprecating the ill-timed frankness, Philoxenus made a paradoxical promise. For he said that by his answer he would preserve at once both the truth and the satisfaction of Dionysius; and he was not false to it.
6.5. For when the tyrant brought forward certain verses containing pitiable sufferings, and asked, "What sort do the poems appear?"—he said, "Pitiful," preserving both meanings through the ambiguity. For Dionysius took "pitiful" to mean piteous and full of compassion, and that such things are the achievements of good poets, whence he received him as having praised him; but the others, taking the true meaning, understood that "pitiful" was said as describing the nature of a failure.
7.1. Something similar happened also in the case of Plato the philosopher. For having sent for this man, at first he deemed him worthy of the greatest acceptance, seeing that he had a frankness worthy of philosophy; but later, taking offence at him over certain discourses, he became wholly estranged, and leading him to the market sold him as a slave for twenty minas. But the philosophers, coming together, bought him out and sent him to Greece, adding the friendly admonition that the wise man should associate with tyrants either as little as possible or as agreeably as possible.
7.2. Dionysius, not desisting from his eagerness for poetry, sent to the Olympic festival the most fine-voiced of the actors to perform his poems among the crowds with song. These at first, because of their fine voices, struck the hearers with amazement, but after this, when reflection set in, they were despised and carried off much laughter.
7.3. Dionysius, hearing of the contempt for his poems, fell into excessive grief; and the affliction ever taking on increase, a maddened disposition seized his soul, and saying that all his friends envied him, he suspected them as plotting. And at last he proceeded to such a pitch of frenzy and derangement that of his friends many he slew on false charges, and not a few he banished; among whom were Philistus and Leptines his brother, men distinguished in valour and who had rendered him many and great services in the wars.
7.4. These, then, fleeing to Thurii in Italy and meeting with great acceptance among the Italiotes, later, at the request of Dionysius, were reconciled, and returning to Syracuse were restored to their former goodwill; and Leptines married the daughter of Dionysius. These things, then, were done in this year.

8.1. In the archonship at Athens of Dexitheus the Romans appointed as consuls Lucius Lucretius and Servius Sulpicius. In this year Evagoras the king of the Salaminians came to Cyprus from Egypt, conveying money from Acoris the king of Egypt, less than had been expected. Finding Salamis vigorously besieged and being abandoned by his allies, he was compelled to send an embassy about a settlement.
8.2. Tiribazus, who had the command of the whole, said that he would agree to the settlement if Evagoras would withdraw from all the cities in Cyprus, and, reigning over Salamis alone, would pay to the King of the Persians a fixed tribute each year and do what was commanded, as a slave to a master.
8.3. Evagoras, although the terms were heavy, agreed to all the rest, but objected to doing what was commanded as a slave to a master, and said that he ought to be subject as a king to a king. Tiribazus not agreeing, Orontes the other general, envying the reputation of Tiribazus, sent letters secretly to Artaxerxes against Tiribazus.
8.4. He accused him, first, that, being able to take Salamis, he did not accomplish this, but received an embassy from Evagoras and conferred about a common undertaking; and likewise that he was privately making an alliance with the Lacedaemonians, being a friend of theirs; and that he had sent certain men to Delphi to ask the god about a rising; and the greatest thing, that he was making the commanders of the forces his own by goodwill, winning them over by honours and gifts and besides by promises.
8.5. The King, reading the letter and trusting the slanders, wrote to Orontes to arrest Tiribazus and send him to himself. He doing what was commanded, Tiribazus, brought up to the King and demanding to obtain a trial, was for the present given over to prison, but after this, the King having a war against the Cadusii and putting off the trial, the matters of the tribunal were dragged out.
9.1. Orontes, succeeding to the command of the forces in Cyprus, and seeing Evagoras again confidently enduring the siege, and besides this the soldiers ill enduring the arrest of Tiribazus, and on this account disobeying and abandoning the siege, Orontes, fearing the strangeness of the situation, sent to Evagoras men to confer about the settlement and to bid him conclude the peace on the terms on which he had thought fit to agree with Tiribazus.
9.2. Evagoras, then, unexpectedly escaped the capture, and concluded the peace, so as to reign over Salamis and to give the fixed tribute each year and to obey, as a king a king who commanded. The Cyprian War, then, which had lasted almost ten years, and most of the time had been occupied with preparations, having for two years at the end been continuously fought, was dissolved in this manner.
9.3. Glos, who had the admiralship of the fleet, having married the daughter of Tiribazus, being greatly afraid lest, seeming to have cooperated with Tiribazus in the affair, he should meet with punishment from the King, resolved by a new undertaking of affairs to secure his own position. Being well supplied with money and soldiers, and besides having made the trierarchs his own by goodwill, he resolved to revolt from the King.
9.4. Immediately, then, sending an embassy to Acoris the king of the Egyptians, he made an alliance against the King, and writing to the Lacedaemonians he stirred them up against the King, and promised to give a quantity of money and made the other great promises, undertaking to assist them in their affairs in Greece and to help them recover their ancestral leadership.
9.5. The Spartans had long since resolved to recover their leadership, and were now already throwing the cities into disorder and were manifest to all as enslaving the cities. Besides this, being in ill repute for seeming, in the agreement with the King, to have given up the Greeks in Asia, they repented of what had been done and sought a plausible pretext for the war against Artaxerxes. Therefore they gladly concluded the alliance with Glos.
10.1. Artaxerxes, having ended the war against the Cadusii, set up the trial for Tiribazus, and appointed three judges of those most esteemed among the Persians. About these times other judges, seeming to have judged badly, were flayed alive, and over the judicial seats the skins being stretched, upon these the judges gave judgement, having before their eyes an example of the penalty for judging badly.
10.2. The accusers, then, reading the letter sent by Orontes, said that this was sufficient for accusation; but Tiribazus, against the slander concerning Evagoras, brought forward the agreement made by Orontes that Evagoras should obey the King as a king a king, while he himself had concluded the peace so that Evagoras should obey the King as a slave a master; and concerning the oracles he said that the god gives no responses at all about death, and of this he produced as witnesses all the Greeks who were present. Concerning the friendship with the Lacedaemonians he made his defence, saying that he had made the friendship not for his own advantage but for the King's profit; and through this he showed that from the Lacedaemonians the Greeks in Asia had been taken away and given over to the King. At the end of his defence he reminded the judges of the services with which he had earlier benefited the King.
10.3. It is said that he had rendered many other services to the King, but one greatest, from which it came to pass that he was admired and became his greatest friend; for during a certain hunt, while the King was being carried on a chariot, two lions rushed upon him, and tore apart two of the horses in the four-horse team, and made their rush against the King himself; at which moment Tiribazus, appearing, both slew the lions and rescued the King from the dangers.
10.4. They say also that in the wars he excelled in valour and in counsels was so successful in aim that the King, using his recommendations, never failed. Tiribazus, having used such a defence, was acquitted of the charges by the agreed verdict of all the judges.

11.1. The King, summoning the judges one by one, asked on what grounds of justice each had acquitted the accused. The first said that he saw the charges disputed, but the benefactions acknowledged; the second said that, even granting the charges to be true, nevertheless the benefactions were greater than the offence; the third said that he did not put the benefactions to account, because Tiribazus had received from the King favours and honours many times over for them, but that, the charges themselves being considered by themselves, the accused did not appear to be liable to them.
11.2. The King praised the judges as having judged justly, and adorned Tiribazus with the greatest customary honours; while of Orontes, having condemned him as having fabricated a false accusation, he excluded him from his friends and surrounded him with the utmost dishonours. And the affairs in Asia were in this state.
12.1. In Greece, the Lacedaemonians ravaging Mantinea, throughout the summer the Mantineans continued fighting nobly against the enemy; for they seemed to excel the Arcadians in valour, and for this reason the Lacedaemonians had earlier been accustomed in their battles to have these as comrades-in-arms and the most faithful of their allies; but when winter set in, and the river by Mantinea took a great increase from the rains, the Lacedaemonians, blocking the stream of the river with great mounds, turned the river into the city and made all the nearby ground a lake.
12.2. Therefore, the houses falling, the Mantineans, struck with dismay, were compelled to surrender the city to the Lacedaemonians. They, taking it over, did no other harm to the Mantineans, but ordered them to remove into the ancient villages. Therefore they were compelled to raze their own fatherland and to remove into the villages.
13.1. At the same time as these things were being done, in Sicily Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans resolved to found cities on the Adriatic. This he did, planning to make his own the passage called the Ionian, so that he might make the voyage to Epirus safe and have cities of his own where he could anchor ships. For he was eager to sail suddenly with great forces against the regions in Epirus and to plunder the precinct at Delphi, full of much wealth.
13.2. Therefore he made an alliance with the Illyrians through Alcetas the Molossian, who happened to be an exile and staying at Syracuse. The Illyrians having a war, he sent them as allies two thousand soldiers and five hundred suits of Greek armour. The Illyrians distributed the armour to the best of their soldiers, and mingled the soldiers with their own soldiers.
13.3. Having gathered a large force, they invaded Epirus and were bringing back Alcetas to the kingdom of the Molossians. No one heeding them, at first they ravaged the country, but after this, the Molossians arraying against them, there was a fierce battle, in which the Illyrians, conquering, cut down more than fifteen thousand of the Molossians. So great a calamity having befallen the Epirotes, the Lacedaemonians, learning what had happened, sent an alliance to the Molossians, by which they put an end to the great boldness of the barbarians.
13.4. At the same time as these things were being done, the Parians, in accordance with a certain oracle, sending out a colony to the Adriatic, founded in it the island named Pharos, Dionysius the tyrant cooperating with them. For he, having sent out a colony to the Adriatic not many years before, had founded the city named Lissus.
13.5. Setting out from this, then, Dionysius . . . having leisure, constructed dockyards for two hundred triremes, and threw about the city a wall of such great magnitude that the circuit became the greatest of the Greek cities. He constructed also great gymnasia by the river Anapus, and built temples of the gods and the other things conducing to the increase and glory of a city.
14.1. The annual period having passed, at Athens Diotrephes was archon, and at Rome were appointed as consuls Lucius Valerius and Aulus Manlius, and among the Eleians the ninety-ninth Olympiad was celebrated, in which Dicon the Syracusan was victor in the stadion. In this year the Parians, having settled Pharos, allowed the barbarians who dwelt there before, being in a place exceedingly strong, to dwell unharmed, while they themselves, founding a city by the sea, walled it.
14.2. After this, the barbarians who dwelt before on the island being displeased at the presence of the Greeks, and sending for the Illyrians dwelling opposite, with many small boats they crossed over to Pharos, being above ten thousand, and plundering the Greeks slew many. But the prefect appointed at Lissus by Dionysius, having many triremes, sailed against the small boats of the Illyrians, and sinking some and mastering others, slew of the barbarians more than five thousand, and took alive about two thousand.
14.3. Dionysius, being in want of money, campaigned against Tyrrhenia, having sixty triremes, putting forward as a pretext the suppression of pirates, but in truth to plunder a holy temple, full of many dedications, set up in the harbour of the city Agylla in Tyrrhenia; the harbour was named Pyrgi.
14.4. Sailing in by night and disembarking his force, falling upon them at daybreak he mastered his undertaking; for there being few guards in the place, overpowering them he plundered the temple and gathered not less than a thousand talents. The Agyllaeans coming to the rescue, he both conquered them in battle and, taking many prisoners and plundering the country, returned to Syracuse. Selling the spoils, he gathered not less than five hundred talents. Being well supplied with money, he hired a multitude of soldiers of every kind, and constituting a considerable force was manifestly about to make war on the Carthaginians. These things, then, were done in this year.

15.1. In the archonship at Athens of Phanostratus the Romans appointed in place of the consuls four military tribunes, Lucius Lucretius, Sentius Sulpicius, Lucius Aemilius, Lucius Furius. In this year Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans, having prepared to make war on the Carthaginians, sought to take a plausible pretext for the war. Seeing, then, that the cities ranged under the Carthaginians were favourably disposed toward revolt, he received those who wished to revolt, and concluding an alliance with them dealt fairly with them.
15.2. The Carthaginians at first, sending envoys to the ruler, demanded back the cities, but when he paid no heed it came to pass that this was the beginning of the war. The Carthaginians, then, making an alliance with the Italiotes, took up the war in common against the tyrant; and prudently foreseeing the magnitude of the war, they both enrolled as soldiers the fit men of their citizens and, having provided a quantity of money, hired great foreign forces. Appointing as general Mago the king, they transported many myriads of soldiers into Sicily and Italy, wishing to fight it out from both sides.
15.3. Dionysius also, dividing his forces, with one part contended against the Italiotes and with the other against the Phoenicians. Many partial battles took place for the armies, and small and continual skirmishes, in which no noteworthy deed was accomplished; but two great and famous engagements occurred. In the first, Dionysius, fighting wonderfully, had the advantage near the place called Cabala, and slew more than ten thousand of the barbarians, and took alive not fewer than five thousand; and the rest of the multitude he forced to flee to a certain strong and wholly waterless hill. Mago too, their king, fell, fighting brilliantly.
15.4. The Phoenicians, struck with dismay at the magnitude of the calamity, immediately sent an embassy about a settlement. Dionysius declared that there was for them one settlement only, if they would withdraw from the cities in Sicily and pay the money expended during the war.
16.1. The answer seeming to be heavy and arrogant, the Carthaginians, with their usual cunning, outgeneralled Dionysius. Pretending to be content with the agreements, they said that they themselves were not masters of the surrender of the cities, but in order that they might confer with the magistrates about these things, they asked Dionysius to make a few days' truce.
16.2. The ruler agreeing, and the truce being made, Dionysius was overjoyed, as about immediately to receive all Sicily, while the Carthaginians buried Mago the king magnificently, and in his place appointed as general his son, who was wholly young, but full of spirit and distinguished in valour. This man, throughout the whole time of the truce, continued drawing up and exercising the force, and through the training in labours and the exhortation of speeches and exercise in arms made the army obedient and capable.
16.3. When the time of the agreement had passed, both sides, drawing up their forces, went down eagerly to battle. A fierce engagement taking place near the place called Cronium, the divinity by an exchange corrected the defeat of the Carthaginians with victory; for those who had conquered before, being boastful because of their previous success, were unexpectedly worsted, while those who had fallen in their hopes because of the defeat carried off an unexpected and great success.
17.1. For Leptines, stationed on the one wing and distinguished in valour, fighting heroically and slaying many of the Carthaginians, ended his life conspicuously; and when he had fallen, the Phoenicians, taking courage and forcing those arrayed against them, routed them.
17.2. Dionysius at first, having the chosen men drawn up with him, had the advantage over those arrayed against him; but when the death of Leptines became known and the other wing had been crushed, the men of Dionysius were struck with dismay and rushed to flight.
17.3. A complete rout taking place, the Carthaginians, pursuing the more eagerly, ordered one another to take no one alive; therefore, all who were overtaken being slain, every nearby place was filled with corpses.
17.4. So great was the slaughter, the Phoenicians bearing malice, that the slain of the Sicilians were found to be more than fourteen thousand. The survivors, fleeing to the camp, were saved when night came on. The Carthaginians, having conquered in a great engagement, withdrew to Panormus.
17.5. Bearing their success humanely, they sent envoys, giving Dionysius leave to end the war. The tyrant gladly receiving the words, a settlement was made, so that both sides should have what they had formerly been masters of; but as a special acquisition the Carthaginians took the city and territory of the Selinuntians and of the Acragantine territory as far as the river called Halycus. And Dionysius paid the Carthaginians a thousand talents. And the affairs in Sicily were in this state.

18.1. In Asia Glos, who had been admiral of the Persians in the Cyprian War, being a rebel from the King and having called upon both the Lacedaemonians and the king of the Egyptians to the war against the Persians, was treacherously slain by certain men and did not accomplish his purpose. After his death Tachos, succeeding to his undertakings, gathered a force about himself, and founded a city near the sea on a certain cliff, named Leuce, which had a holy temple of Apollo.
18.2. A little while later, he having died, the Clazomenians and Cymaeans disputed over this city. At first the cities attempted to decide by war, but after this, someone proposing to ask the god which of the cities he judged ought to be mistress of Leuce, the Pythia decided that it should be whichever first sacrificed at Leuce; and that they should set out from their own city at sunrise on the day which both should by agreement fix.
18.3. The day having been appointed, the Cymaeans supposed that they had the advantage because their city lay nearer; but the Clazomenians, being a greater distance off, contrived something of this sort for the victory: choosing by lot colonists from among themselves, they founded a city near Leuce, from which, setting out at sunrise, they forestalled the Cymaeans in completing the sacrifice.
18.4. By this device, having become masters of Leuce, they established the holding of an eponymous festival each year, naming the festival Prophthaseia (the Forestalling). These things being done, the risings in Asia were of themselves dissolved.
19.1. The Lacedaemonians, after the death of Glos and Tachos, gave up the affairs in Asia, and arranging the affairs in Greece, and bringing over some of the cities by persuasion, and others by force through the return of exiles mastering them, were now openly transferring to themselves the leadership of Greece, contrary to the common treaties made under Antalcidas with the cooperation of the King of the Persians.
19.2. In Macedonia, Amyntas the king, being defeated by the Illyrians and despairing of his rule, and besides this having given to the people of the Olynthians much of the bordering country because of his despair of his own dominion, at first the people of the Olynthians received the revenues from the country given; but after this, the King unexpectedly recovering himself and regaining his whole rule, the Olynthians, being asked back for the country, were not willing to give it up.
19.3. Therefore Amyntas both constituted his own force and, making the Lacedaemonians allies, persuaded them to send out a general and a considerable force against the Olynthians. The Lacedaemonians, deciding to hold to the regions in Thrace, enrolled soldiers both from the citizens and from the allies, in all above ten thousand; and handing over the force to Phoebidas the Spartan, they ordered him to ally himself with Amyntas and with him to make war on the Olynthians. Sending another force against the Phliasians and conquering them in battle, they compelled the Phliasians to submit to the Lacedaemonians.
19.4. About this time the kings of the Lacedaemonians differed with one another in their inclinations. For Agesipolis, being peaceful and just, and besides distinguished in understanding, said that they ought to abide by their oaths and not, contrary to the common treaties, enslave the Greeks; for he declared that Sparta was in ill repute, having given over to the Persians the Greeks in Asia, while herself arranging the cities in Greece, after swearing in the common treaties to keep them independent. But Agesilaus, being by nature energetic, was warlike and clung to the dominion of the Greeks.

20.1. In the archonship at Athens of Evander the Romans appointed in place of the consuls six military tribunes, Quintus Sulpicius, Gaius Fabius, Quintus Servilius, Publius Cornelius. In this year the Lacedaemonians seized the Cadmeia in Thebes for some such causes as these. Seeing Boeotia to have a multitude of cities, and the men dwelling in it to be distinguished in valour, and besides Thebes to have an ancient dignity and in sum to be like a citadel of Boeotia, they were on their guard lest, if ever a fit occasion appeared, it should lay claim to the leadership;
20.2. therefore the Spartans gave secret orders to their commanders that, if ever they should get an opportunity, they should seize the Cadmeia. Such an order having been given, Phoebidas the Spartan, appointed to a command and leading a force against the Olynthians, seized the Cadmeia. The Thebans being indignant and running together with arms, joining battle with them and conquering, he banished three hundred of the most notable of the Thebans, and striking dismay into the rest and establishing a strong garrison, departed to his own affairs. The Lacedaemonians, being in ill repute among the Greeks because of this deed, fined Phoebidas a sum of money, but did not lead the garrison out of Thebes;
20.3. the Thebans, then, in this manner losing their independence, were compelled to submit to the Lacedaemonians. The Olynthians being at war with Amyntas the king of the Macedonians, the Lacedaemonians removed Phoebidas from the command and appointed as general Eudamidas the brother of Phoebidas. Giving him three thousand hoplites, they sent him out to fight the war against the Olynthians.
21.1. He, invading the country of the Olynthians, in common with Amyntas fought the war against the Olynthians. Then the Olynthians, having gathered a considerable force, had the advantage in the battles, having more soldiers than the enemy; but the Lacedaemonians, providing a considerable force, appointed as general over it Teleutias. This man was the brother of Agesilaus the king, and was admired for his virtue among the citizens.
21.2. Setting out, then, with a force from the Peloponnese and coming near the Olynthians, he took over the soldiers under Eudamidas. Being a match for battle, at first he ravaged the country of the Olynthians, and gathering a quantity of booty distributed it to the soldiers. The Olynthians with their allies arraying in full force, he joined battle. And at first, the contest being even, they parted; but after this, a fierce battle taking place, Teleutias himself fell, fighting brilliantly, and of the Lacedaemonians more than twelve hundred were slain.
21.3. So great a success having come to the Olynthians, the Lacedaemonians, wishing to correct the reverse that had occurred, prepared to send out larger forces, while the Olynthians, thinking that the Spartans would come with greater forces and that the war would be long, made considerable preparations of grain and took on soldiers from the allies.
22.1. In the archonship at Athens of Demophilus the Romans appointed in place of the consuls military tribunes, Publius Cornelius, Lucius Verginius, Lucius Papirius, Marcus Furius, Valerius, Aulus Manlius, Lucius and Postumius.
22.2. In this year the Lacedaemonians, providing as general Agesipolis the king, and giving him a sufficient force, voted to make war on the Olynthians. He, coming to the country of the Olynthians and taking over the soldiers already in the camp, fought the war against the natives. The Olynthians constituted no great battle in this year, but continued making skirmishes and brief encounters, struck with dismay at the force with the king.

23.1. The annual period having passed, at Athens the archon was Pytheas, and at Rome six military tribunes were appointed in place of the consuls, Titus Quinctius, Lucius Servilius, Lucius Julius, Aquillius, Lucius Lucretius, Servius Sulpicius, and among the Eleians the hundredth Olympiad was celebrated, in which Dionysodorus the Tarentine was victor in the stadion.
23.2. In this year Agesipolis the king of the Lacedaemonians died of disease, having reigned fourteen years; and his rule was succeeded by Cleombrotus his brother, who reigned nine years. The Lacedaemonians, appointing Polybiades as general, sent him out to the war against the Olynthians.
23.3. He, taking over the forces and managing the war both vigorously and skilfully, made many advances. Ever succeeding more and conquering in several battles, he shut up the Olynthians in a siege; and at last, striking dismay into the enemy, he ordered them to submit to the Lacedaemonians. The Olynthians being enrolled in the alliance of the Spartans, many also of the other cities were eager to be enrolled under the leadership of the Lacedaemonians. Therefore at these times the Lacedaemonians had the greatest strength, and held the leadership of Greece both by land and by sea.
23.4. For the Thebans were under garrison, and the Corinthians and Argives, because of their previous wars, were humbled, and the Athenians, because of the cleruchies imposed on those they had subdued, were in ill repute among the Greeks; while the Lacedaemonians took much forethought both for their populousness and for their practice in arms, and were fearsome to all because of the power of their leadership.
23.5. Therefore the greatest of the rulers of that time, I mean the King of the Persians and Dionysius the ruler of Sicily, courted the leadership of the Spartans and were eager to conclude an alliance with them.
24.1. In the archonship at Athens of Nicon the Romans appointed six military tribunes in place of the consuls, Lucius Papirius, Gaius Servilius, Lucius Quinctius, Lucius Cornelius, Lucius Valerius, Aulus Manlius. In this year the Carthaginians, campaigning into Italy, restored to the Hipponiatae, who had been driven from their fatherland, their city, and gathering together all who had fled, took much care of them.
24.2. After this, a pestilential disease having befallen the inhabitants of Carthage, and the disease having great increase, many of the Carthaginians perished, and they were in danger of losing their leadership; for both the Libyans, despising them, revolted, and the inhabitants of Sardinia, thinking they had an opportunity against the Carthaginians, revolted from them and, conspiring together, attacked the Carthaginians.
24.3. There occurred about the same time a god-sent misfortune in Carthage. For disturbances and fears and panic tumults occurred continually throughout the city, strange and unaccountable, and many rushed out of their houses with arms, as though enemies had broken into the city, and fighting against one another as enemies, some they slew, some they wounded. At last, having propitiated the divinity with sacrifices and with difficulty being rid of their ills, they quickly both subdued the Libyans and recovered the island.

25.1. In the archonship at Athens of Nausinicus the Romans appointed four military tribunes in place of the consuls, Marcus Cornelius and Quintus Servilius, Marcus Furius and Lucius Quinctius. In this year the so-called Boeotian War arose for the Lacedaemonians against the Boeotians for some such causes as these. The Lacedaemonians garrisoning the Cadmeia unjustly and having banished many of the notable men, the exiles banded together, and with the cooperation of the Athenians returned to their fatherland by night.
25.2. And first they slew in their own houses those who favoured the Lacedaemonians, catching them still asleep; then, calling the citizens to freedom, they had as cooperators all the Thebans. Quickly the multitude running together with arms, at daybreak they attempted to besiege the Cadmeia.
25.3. The Lacedaemonians garrisoning the citadel, being with their allies not fewer than fifteen hundred, sent to Sparta those who should declare the rising of the Thebans and call for help as quickly as possible, while they themselves, defending from commanding positions against the besiegers, slew many and wounded not a few.
25.4. The Thebans, expecting that a great force would come from Greece for the Lacedaemonians, sent envoys to Athens, reminding them that they too had helped restore the people of the Athenians at the time when they were enslaved by the Thirty Tyrants, and asking them to help in full force and, before the arrival of the Lacedaemonians, to help take the Cadmeia.
26.1. The people of the Athenians, having heard the envoys, voted at once to send out as great a force as possible to free Thebes, both rendering the thanks for the benefaction and at the same time wishing to make the Boeotians their own and to have strong fellow-fighters against the supremacy of the Lacedaemonians; for this nation, both in the multitude of its men and in valour in war, seemed to fall behind none of the Greek peoples.
26.2. At last Demophon, appointed general, and at once enrolling five thousand hoplites and five hundred horse, on the next day led the force out of the city at daybreak, and hastened at a run, eager to forestall the Lacedaemonians; and the people none the less prepared to campaign in full force into Boeotia, if there should be need.
26.3. Demophon, using short roads, unexpectedly appeared to the Thebans. Likewise also from the other cities in Boeotia, many soldiers running together, quickly a great force was gathered for the Thebans.
26.4. For hoplites came together not fewer than twelve thousand, and horsemen more than two thousand. All eagerly setting about the siege, dividing the multitude, they made the assaults in relays, persevering in the dangers continually both day and night.
27.1. Those garrisoning the Cadmeia, exhorted by their commanders, vigorously defended themselves against the enemy, hoping that the Lacedaemonians would shortly come with a great force. So long, then, as they had sufficient food, they held out against the dangers, and slew and wounded many of the besiegers, having as their helper the strength of the citadel; but when the scarcity of necessaries grew acute, and the Lacedaemonians, being occupied with preparations, delayed, they fell into faction with one another.
27.2. For the Lacedaemonians thought they ought to hold out to the death, but those who had campaigned from the allied cities, being many times more, declared for surrendering the Cadmeia; and those from Sparta itself, being few, were compelled to give up the citadel. Therefore these, released under truce by agreement, departed to the Peloponnese;
27.3. but the Lacedaemonians, advancing with considerable forces against Thebes, and being a little late for the occasion, had their undertaking fruitless. The commanders of the garrison, being three, they brought to trial, and condemned two to death, while the third they fined so great a sum of money that his property could not pay so much.
27.4. After this the Athenians returned to their fatherland, and the Thebans, besieging Thespiae, had their undertaking fruitless. At the same time as these things were being done, the Romans sent five hundred colonists, free of taxes, to Sardinia.

28.1. In the archonship at Athens of Calleas the Romans appointed in place of the consuls four military tribunes, Lucius Papirius, Marcus Publius, Titus Cornelius, Quintus Lucius. In this year, the Lacedaemonians having stumbled about Thebes, the Boeotians, taking courage, banded together, and making a common alliance constituted a considerable force, expecting that the Lacedaemonians would come with great forces into Boeotia.
28.2. The Athenians sent the most notable of their men as envoys to the cities ranged under the Lacedaemonians, calling on them to hold to the common freedom. For the Lacedaemonians, because of the magnitude of their power, ruled their subjects contemptuously and harshly; therefore many of those ranged under them inclined toward the Athenians.
28.3. First to obey the call to revolt were the Chians and Byzantines, and after these the Rhodians and Mitylenaeans and certain others of the islanders; the impulse of the Greeks ever increasing, many cities attached themselves to the Athenians. The people, lifted up by the goodwill of the cities, constituted a common council of all the allies, and appointed councillors from each city.
28.4. It was arranged by common consent that the council should meet at Athens, that a city, equally great and small, should have authority over a single vote, that all should be independent, using the Athenians as leaders. The Lacedaemonians, seeing the impulse of the cities toward revolt to be uncontrollable, nevertheless by embassies and humane speeches, and besides by beneficent promises, were ambitious to correct the estrangement of the men.
28.5. Likewise they took much thought also for their preparation for the war, expecting that the Boeotian War would be great and long for them, the Athenians and the other Greeks who shared in the council being allied with the Thebans.
29.1. At the same time as these things were being done, Acoris the king of the Egyptians, being ill disposed toward the King of the Persians, gathered considerable foreign forces; for, offering great wages to those who obeyed and benefiting many, he quickly had many of the Greeks obeying for the campaign.
29.2. Not having a general of sufficient worth, he sent for Chabrias the Athenian, a man distinguished both in prudence and in generalship's understanding, and who had won a great reputation for virtue. He, then, without the consent of the people, having accepted the command, led the forces in Egypt, and with much eagerness prepared to make war on the Persians.
29.3. Pharnabazus, designated by the King as general over the Persian force, made great preparations of the things useful for the war; and he sent envoys to the Athenians, accusing Chabrias, that, leading the Egyptians, he was estranging the King's goodwill from the people, and asking them to give him Iphicrates as general.
29.4. The Athenians, eager to bring the King of the Persians into goodwill and to make Pharnabazus their own, quickly both sent for Chabrias from Egypt and sent out Iphicrates as general to ally himself with the Persians.
29.5. The Lacedaemonians and the Athenians, having made a treaty in the times above, it came to pass that the peace remained until these times. After this, Sphodriades the Spartan being appointed to a command, and being by nature excitable and rash, Cleombrotus the king of the Lacedaemonians persuaded him, without the consent of the ephors, to seize the Piraeus.
29.6. Sphodriades, having more than ten thousand soldiers, attempted by night to seize the Piraeus; but becoming visible to the Athenians and failing of his undertaking, he returned fruitless. Being accused in the council of the Spartans, and having the kings as supporters, he was unjustly acquitted.
29.7. Therefore the Athenians, taking it ill at what had happened, voted that the treaty had been broken by the Lacedaemonians. Deciding to make war on them, they chose three generals, the most notable of the citizens, Timotheus and Chabrias and Callistratus. They voted to enroll as soldiers twenty thousand hoplites and five hundred horse, and to man two hundred ships. They also took the Thebans into the common council on equal terms in all things.
29.8. They voted also to restore the cleruchies that had been made to those who had earlier been masters, and they passed a law that none of the Athenians should farm outside Attica. Through this humanity, having recovered the goodwill among the Greeks, they made their own leadership stronger.

30.1. Many also of the other cities for the aforesaid reason were prompted to incline toward the Athenians, and first and most eagerly those dwelling in Euboea allied themselves, except Hestiaea; for this city, having been greatly benefited by the Lacedaemonians, but terribly warred upon by the Athenians, reasonably kept its enmity toward the Athenians undissolved, and toward the Spartans preserved its faith firm.
30.2. Nevertheless, seventy cities came over into alliance with the Athenians and shared on equal terms in the common council; therefore, the power of the Athenians ever increasing more and that of the Lacedaemonians being humbled, it came to pass that the strength of the cities became evenly matched. The Athenians, their affairs proceeding according to their mind, sent a force into Euboea to guard the allies and to subdue their opponents.
30.3. In Euboea, a little before these times, a certain man named Neogenes, with Jason of Pherae, having collected soldiers, seized the citadel of the Hestiaeans, and declared himself tyrant of this country and of the city of the Oreitae. He ruling violently and arrogantly, the Lacedaemonians sent Theripides against him.
30.4. He at first attempted by words to make the tyrant withdraw from the citadel; but when he paid no heed, calling the natives to freedom he took the place by siege and restored to the Oreitae their freedom; for which reason those dwelling in the country called the Hestiaeotid were favourably disposed toward the Spartans, and firmly kept the friendship.
30.5. Chabrias, leading the force sent out by the Athenians, ravaged the Hestiaeotid country, and the place called Metropolis, lying on a certain strong hill, he walled and left in it a garrison, while he himself, sailing against the Cyclades islands, brought over Peparethos and Sciathos and certain others that were ranged under the Lacedaemonians.
31.1. The Lacedaemonians, seeing the impulse of the allies toward revolt to be uncontrollable, ceased from their former harshness and dealt humanely with the cities. By such associations and benefactions they made all the allies better disposed. Seeing the war increasing and requiring much attention, they made the other preparations zealously and worked out the arrangement and division of the soldiers and the public services rather elaborately.
31.2. For the cities and the soldiers enrolled for the war they divided into ten parts. Of these the Lacedaemonians held the first part, the Arcadians the second and third, the Eleians the fourth, the Achaeans the fifth; the Corinthians and Megarians filled the sixth, the Sicyonians and Phliasians and those dwelling in the place called Acte the seventh, the Acarnanians the eighth, the Phocians and Locrians the ninth, and the Olynthians and the allies dwelling in Thrace the last. For them the hoplite was reckoned as against two light-armed, and the horseman as equal to four hoplites.
31.3. Such being the arrangement, the army was led by Agesilaus the king; he was renowned for valour and generalship's understanding and had been almost unconquered in the times above. For both in the other wars he was admired, and at the time when the Lacedaemonians made war on the Persians, having drawn up and conquered a force many times larger, he went over much of Asia, mastering the open country, and finally, had not the Spartans summoned him for certain political needs, he would almost have brought the whole kingdom of the Persians into the utmost dangers.
31.4. For this man was energetic, and with much understanding bold and using daring deeds. Therefore at that time the Spartans, seeing the magnitude of the war requiring a considerable leader, appointed this man leader of the whole war.
32.1. Agesilaus, leading forward the force, came into Boeotia, having in all soldiers more than eighteen thousand, of whom were five divisions of the Lacedaemonians; and the division is filled by five hundred men. The company called the Sciritae among the Spartans is not drawn up with the others, but having its own constitution stands with the king, and comes to the aid of whatever parts are at any time hard pressed; being composed of chosen men, it makes great turns in the engagements and is for the most part the cause of the victory. Agesilaus had fifteen hundred horse.
32.2. He, then, coming to the city Thespiae, garrisoned by the Lacedaemonians, encamped near it, and refreshed the soldiers for some days from their hardship. The Athenians, learning of the presence of the Lacedaemonians in Boeotia, immediately came to the aid of Thebes, having five thousand foot and two hundred horse.
32.3. These forces being gathered into one place, the Thebans seized a certain oblong hill, distant twenty stades from the city, and making the difficult ground their defence, awaited the onset of the enemy; for, struck with dismay at the reputation of Agesilaus, they were on their guard against an even contest on the plains.
32.4. Agesilaus, leading his force in order against the Boeotians, when he drew near the enemy, at first sent the light-armed against his opponents, trying how they stood toward battle. The Thebans easily beating these off from commanding positions, he led the whole force in order against them strikingly.
32.5. Chabrias the Athenian, leading the mercenaries, ordered the soldiers to receive the enemy contemptuously and at the same time in order, and, leaning their shields against the knee with spear upright, to remain.
32.6. They doing what was commanded as if at a single word of command, Agesilaus, marvelling at both the good order of the enemy and the contempt, did not decide to force his way against commanding positions and to compel his opponents, being brave men, to become valiant for hand-to-hand danger, but having made trial that they would dare to fight it out for the victory when forced, he challenged them in the plain. The Thebans not coming down, he led away the phalanx of foot, and sending out the cavalry and the light-armed of the companies he ravaged the country without fear and became master of much booty.

33.1. The Spartan counsellors who were with Agesilaus and those holding the commands marvelled how Agesilaus, seeming to be energetic and having a larger and more powerful force, did not fight it out with the enemy. To them Agesilaus answered that now the Lacedaemonians had conquered without danger; for, the country being ravaged, the Boeotians had not dared to come to its aid; but if, the enemy themselves having yielded the victory, he had forced the enemy to face the danger, perhaps, through the unaccountableness of fortune, the Lacedaemonians might even have stumbled in the contest.
33.2. At that time, then, by this answer he seemed to have guessed moderately what might come to pass; but later, through the outcomes, he seemed to have spoken not a human declaration, but a kind of divine oracle. For the Lacedaemonians, campaigning with a great force against the Thebans and compelling them to fight for their freedom, fell into a great calamity.
33.3. For first at Leuctra, being defeated, they lost many of their citizens, among whom their king Cleombrotus also fell; and after this, fighting at Mantinea, they were utterly worsted and lost their leadership beyond hope. For fortune is good at unexpectedly tripping up the high-minded and teaching them to hope for nothing too greatly. Agesilaus, at any rate, prudently being content with the first advantage, kept his force unharmed.
33.4. After this, Agesilaus with his force returned to the Peloponnese, while the Thebans, saved through the generalship of Chabrias, marvelled at the man's quickness of wit in the stratagem. Chabrias, although many noble things had been done by him in war, prided himself most on this stratagem, and set up the statues given him by the people in this posture.
33.5. The Thebans, after the departure of Agesilaus, campaigning against Thespiae, slew the advance guard, being two hundred men, and making continual assaults on the city, but accomplishing nothing noteworthy, led the force back to Thebes.
33.6. Phoebidas the Lacedaemonian, having a considerable garrison in Thespiae, pouring out of the city and rashly attacking the withdrawing Thebans, lost more than five hundred of his soldiers, while he himself, fighting brilliantly and falling in with many wounds in front, ended his life heroically.
34.1. Not long afterward, the Lacedaemonians again campaigning with the same force against Thebes, the Thebans, seizing certain other difficult positions, prevented the enemy from plundering the country, but did not dare to array against the whole force in the plains.
34.2. Agesilaus pressing on, they came down little by little to the contest. A battle taking place, fierce for a long time, at first the men of Agesilaus had the advantage, but after this, the Thebans from the city pouring out in full force, Agesilaus, seeing the multitude of those streaming in, recalled the soldiers from the battle by the trumpet. The Thebans, thinking they were then for the first time not inferior to the Lacedaemonians, both set up a trophy and for the rest took courage against the force of the Spartans.
34.3. The affairs concerning the infantry forces, then, had such an end; and of the naval forces about the same time there occurred a great sea-battle between Naxos and Paros for some such causes as these. Pollis the admiral of the Lacedaemonians, learning that a quantity of grain was being conveyed in merchant-ships to the Athenians, lay in wait and watched for the arrival of the conveyed provisions, planning to attack the merchant-ships. The people of the Athenians, learning this, sent out a fleet to guard the grain-convoy, which also brought the conveyed provisions safe to the Piraeus.
34.4. After this, Chabrias the admiral of the Athenians, sailing with the whole fleet against Naxos, constituted a siege. Bringing up engines to the walls and through these shaking the walls, he brought zeal to master the city by force. At the same time as these things were being done, Pollis the admiral of the Lacedaemonians sailed up to help the Naxians. A rivalry arising, both sides went down to a sea-battle, and drawing up their ships sailed against one another.
34.5. Pollis had sixty-five triremes, and Chabrias eighty-three. The ships sailing against one another, Pollis, leading the right wing, first attacked the triremes arrayed against him on the left wing, of which Cedon the Athenian was leader; fighting brilliantly, he both destroyed Cedon himself and sank his ship; and likewise engaging the others and breaking them up with his rams, some he destroyed, others he forced to flee. Seeing this, Chabrias, sending a part of the ships about him, helped those who were hard pressed and corrected the defeat of his own, while he himself, having the strongest part of the fleet and fighting nobly, destroyed many triremes and took not a few prisoners.
35.1. Being upon his advantage, and having forced all the enemy's ships to flee, he wholly abstained from the pursuit; for remembering the sea-battle at Arginusae, in which the people, in return for a great benefaction, surrounded the victorious generals with death, charging them that they did not bury those who had died in the sea-battle, he was on his guard lest, a like situation arising, he should risk suffering the like. Therefore, desisting from the pursuit, he picked up his citizens who were swimming, and those still living he saved, and those who had died he buried. Had he not been engaged in this care, he would easily have destroyed the whole fleet of the enemy.
35.2. In the sea-battle, of the Athenians eighteen triremes were destroyed, and of the Lacedaemonians twenty-four were destroyed, and eight were taken with all their crews. Chabrias, then, having conquered in a notable sea-battle, sailed with much booty to the Piraeus, and met with great acceptance among the citizens. For after the Peloponnesian War the Athenians won this first sea-battle; for the one off Cnidus they did not fight on their own, but, using the royal fleet, had the advantage.
35.3. At the same time as these things were being done, in Italy at Rome Marcus Manlius, attempting a tyranny and being overcome, was slain.

36.1. In the archonship at Athens of Charisander the Romans appointed in place of the consuls four military tribunes, Servius Sulpicius, Lucius Papirius, Titus Quinctius, and the Eleians celebrated the hundred-and-first Olympiad, in which Damon the Thurian was victor in the stadion. In this year in Thrace the Triballi, hard pressed by famine, made a campaign in full force against the country beyond their borders, and provided themselves food from foreign land.
36.2. Being more than thirty thousand, they overran the neighbouring Thrace and ravaged the country of the Abderites without fear; and having gained possession of much booty, they were making their return contemptuously and in disorder. The Abderites, campaigning in full force against them as they were making their return scattered and in disorder, slew more than two thousand.
36.3. The barbarians, provoked at what had happened, and wishing to take vengeance on the Abderites, again invaded their country. Those who had won before, lifted up by their advantage, and the neighbouring Thracians having sent them an alliance, arrayed against the barbarians.
36.4. A fierce battle taking place, and the Thracians suddenly changing sides, the Abderites, left alone and surrounded by the multitude of the barbarians, were almost all of those who had shared in the battle cut down. So great a calamity having befallen the Abderites, and they being about to be besieged, Chabrias the Athenian, appearing with a force, rescued the Abderites from the dangers, and drove the barbarians out of the country, and leaving in the city a considerable garrison was himself treacherously slain by certain men.
36.5. Timotheus, taking over the admiralship and sailing to Cephallenia, both brought over the cities in it and likewise persuaded those in Acarnania to incline toward the Athenians. Making Alcetas the king of the Molossians a friend, and in general making his own the lands of the cities about those regions, he conquered the Lacedaemonians in a sea-battle off Leucas.
36.6. All these things he accomplished quickly and easily, persuading by the power of his speech and conquering by valour and generalship. Therefore not only among the citizens but also among the other Greeks he met with great acceptance. And the affairs concerning Timotheus were in this state.
37.1. At the same time as these things were being done, the Thebans campaigned against Orchomenus with five hundred chosen men, and accomplished a deed worthy of memory; for the Lacedaemonians garrisoning Orchomenus with many soldiers, and these arraying against the Thebans, a fierce battle took place, in which the Thebans, engaging against twice their number, conquered the Lacedaemonians. For never had it happened in the times above that this came to pass, but it seemed satisfactory for many to conquer few.
37.2. Therefore the Thebans were filled with spirit, and held their valour more renowned, and became manifestly disposed to dispute the leadership of the Greeks.
37.3. Of the historians, Hermeias of Methymna closed his work on Sicilian affairs at this year, having written ten books, or, as some divide them, twelve.

38.1. In the archonship at Athens of Hippodamus the Romans appointed four military tribunes in place of the consuls, Lucius Valerius, Lucius Manlius, Servius Sulpicius, Lucretius. In this year Artaxerxes the King of the Persians, being about to make war on the Egyptians and eager to constitute a considerable foreign force, resolved to settle the wars in Greece; for thus he most hoped that the Greeks, being released from their own wars, would be more ready for the enlistments. Therefore he sent envoys to Greece to call upon the cities to conclude a common peace.
38.2. The Greeks gladly receiving the words, because they were worn down by the continuity of the wars, all concluded the peace, so that all the cities should be independent and ungarrisoned. And the Greeks appointed commissioners of withdrawal, who, going to each city, led out all the garrisons.
38.3. Only the Thebans not consenting that the treaties should be made by city, but ranging all Boeotia under the Theban confederacy, and the Athenians objecting most ambitiously, Callistratus the demagogue setting forth the speech, while on behalf of the Thebans Epaminondas set forth a speech wonderfully in the common council, the treaties were concluded with all the other Greeks in agreement, but the Thebans alone were judged excluded from the treaty, and Epaminondas, through his own virtue inspiring spirit in the citizens, they took courage to oppose the decrees of all.
38.4. For the Lacedaemonians and Athenians, throughout being ambitious over the leadership, yielded to one another, the one being judged worthy of the rule by land, the other of that by sea. Therefore they bore ill the leadership being referred to a third party, and detached the cities in Boeotia from the Theban confederacy.
39.1. The Thebans, distinguished both in the strength of their bodies and in their might, and having conquered the Lacedaemonians in many battles, were high-minded in spirit and disputed the leadership by land. They were not deceived of their hope, for the aforesaid reasons and because they had more good leaders and generals during the times in question.
39.2. The most notable were Pelopidas and Gorgidas and Epaminondas; for this man surpassed far not only his own countrymen but all the Greeks in valour and generalship's understanding. For he had shared to a great extent in all education, and most of all in Pythagorean philosophy; and besides this, being endowed with natural advantages, reasonably he accomplished the most notable deeds. Therefore, even when compelled with few citizen-soldiers to contend against all the forces of the Lacedaemonians and their allies, he so far surpassed the unconquered soldiers that he slew Cleombrotus the king of the Spartans, and almost utterly cut down the multitude of those arrayed against him.

39.3. And he accomplished such great things unexpectedly because of the quickness of wit and the virtue that had come to him from education. But concerning these things we shall make clearer a little later in the parts set forth, and now we shall turn to the continuous narrative of our history.
40.1. For after the independence granted to the peoples, the cities fell into great disturbances and factions, and most of all those in the Peloponnese. For, having used oligarchic constitutions, and using the licences of democracy without good experience, they banished many of the good men and, casting on them sycophantic charges, condemned them. Therefore, falling into factions, they made banishments and confiscations of properties, and most of all against those who had presided over their fatherlands during the leadership of the Lacedaemonians.
40.2. For in those times those men having dealt dictatorially with the citizens, later the democratic crowd, recovering its freedom, bore malice. First the exiles of the Phialeans, banding together, seized the place called Heraea, a strong stronghold. Setting out from this, they burst into Phialeia, and the Dionysia happening to be on, falling unexpectedly upon those sitting in the theatre, and slaughtering many, and persuading not a few to share their desperation, they withdrew to Sparta.
40.3. The exiles of Corinth, many staying among the Argives, attempted to return; received into the city by certain kinsmen and friends, being slandered they became surrounded; and being about to be seized, and fearing the outrage from capture, they killed one another. The Corinthians, charging many of the citizens with having shared in the attempt with the exiles, slew some and banished others.
40.4. In the city of the Megarians some, attempting to change the constitution and being overcome by the people, were slain, many, and not a few were driven out. Likewise also among the Sicyonians some, attempting to revolt and failing, were slain.
40.5. Among the Phliasians, many being banished, and having seized a strong stronghold in the country and gathered a multitude of mercenaries, there was a battle against those from the city, and the exiles conquering, of the Phliasians above three hundred were slain. Later, the guards betraying the exiles, the Phliasians, mastering the exiles, slew more than six hundred, and casting the rest out of the country forced them to flee to Argos. The cities in the Peloponnese, then, were in such misfortunes.
41.1. In the archonship at Athens of Socratides the Romans appointed in place of the consuls four military tribunes, Quintus Servilius, Servius Cornelius, and besides Spurius Papirius. In this year Artaxerxes the King campaigned against the Egyptians who had revolted from the Persians. The forces were led by Pharnabazus of the barbarian forces, and Iphicrates the Athenian of the mercenaries, who were twenty thousand. This man, summoned to the command by the King, was appointed because of his virtue in generalship.
41.2. Pharnabazus having spent several years over the preparations, Iphicrates, seeing him to be clever in speaking but sluggish in action, used frankness toward him, saying that he marvelled how in words he was sharp, but in deeds slow. Pharnabazus answered that of words he himself was master, but of deeds the King.
41.3. The Persian force being gathered at the city Ace, there were numbered of the barbarians twenty myriads, of whom Pharnabazus was leader; and of the mercenary Greeks Iphicrates led twenty thousand. And there were numbered ships, three hundred triremes and two hundred thirty-oared galleys; and of those conveying the provisions and the rest of the supply there was a great number.
41.4. The summer beginning, the King's generals set out with the whole force, and the fleet sailing along, advanced toward Egypt. When they came near the Nile, they found the Egyptians manifestly prepared for the war.
41.5. For Pharnabazus made the campaign slow and had given the enemy much time for preparation. For in general the generals of the Persians, not being masters of the whole, refer everything to the King and wait for the answers about each thing.

42.1. The king of the Egyptians, Nectanebis, learned the magnitude of the Persian forces, but was confident most of all in the strength of the country, Egypt being wholly hard to approach, and then also because all the entrances, both those from land and those from sea, had been well blocked.
42.2. For the Nile making its outlets into the Egyptian sea by seven mouths, at each of the mouths a city had been built, having great towers on each side of the stream and a wooden bridge commanding the entrance. He especially fortified the Pelusiac mouth, because it lies first toward those coming from Syria and it seemed that through this most of all the enemy would make their approach.
42.3. For he dug a trench across this, and walled off the entrances at the most convenient places, and of the approaches he made the land-passable ones into marsh, and the navigable ones he blocked with mounds. Therefore it was not easy either for the ships to sail in or for the cavalry to draw near or for the infantry to approach.
42.4. The generals under Pharnabazus, finding the Pelusiac mouth wonderfully fortified and guarded by a multitude of soldiers, wholly rejected forcing through it, and resolved to make their entrance through another mouth. Therefore, sailing on the open sea so that the ships should not be seen by the enemy, they put in at the mouth called the Mendesian, which had a beach extending over a considerable space. Disembarking there with three thousand soldiers, both Pharnabazus and Iphicrates advanced against the small fortified town on the mouth.
42.5. The Egyptians coming to the rescue with three thousand horse and foot, and a fierce battle taking place, and many having come up to the Persians from the ships, the Egyptians, surrounded, many died, and not a few were taken alive; the survivors were pursued together into the city. Iphicrates and his men, bursting in together with the garrison inside the walls and mastering the stronghold, razed it and enslaved the inhabitants.
43.1. After this faction fell upon the generals, through which they failed of the undertaking. For Iphicrates, learning from the prisoners that Memphis was undefended, being the most strategic city in Egypt, advised sailing up immediately to Memphis before the Egyptian forces should arrive; but Pharnabazus and his men thought they ought to await the whole force of the Persians; for the campaign against Memphis would be safer.
43.2. When Iphicrates asked that the mercenaries present be given to him, and undertook with them to master the city, Pharnabazus suspected his boldness and virtue, lest he hold Egypt for himself. Therefore, Pharnabazus not consenting, Iphicrates protested, saying that if they let pass the sharpness of the occasions they would render the whole campaign fruitless. Some of the generals envied him and attached unjust slanders.
43.3. The Egyptians, gaining much respite, sent to Memphis a sufficient garrison, and coming with all their forces against the plundered fortified town, and having many advantages because of the strength of the places, made continual encounters with the enemy. Ever growing stronger, they slew many of the Persians and took courage against the enemy.
43.4. The campaign about this town being prolonged, and the Etesian winds now having come, the Nile, filling and covering every place with the abundance of its stream, ever more fortified Egypt. The leaders of the Persians, the situation ever working against them, decided to make their departure from Egypt.
43.5. Therefore, as they were returning to Asia, and a difference arising between Pharnabazus and Iphicrates, Iphicrates, suspecting that he might be arrested and meet with punishment, as Conon the Athenian had suffered, resolved to flee secretly from the camp; therefore, having prepared a boat, he departed unobserved by night and sailed to Athens.
43.6. Pharnabazus, sending envoys, accused Iphicrates as having been the cause of Egypt not being taken. The Athenians gave the Persians the answer that, if they found him to have done wrong, they would punish him according to his deserts; but they themselves, a little time later, appointed Iphicrates general over the fleet.

44.1. It is not foreign to set down the things recorded about the virtue of Iphicrates. For this man is handed down to have had a generalship's quickness of wit and to have used by nature a distinguished gift toward every good device. Taking on, then, in the Persian War the long experience of soldierly works, he devised many things useful for war, and especially was ambitious about the equipment.
44.2. For the Greeks using great shields and on this account being hard to move, he reduced the shields and constructed pelta of moderate size, aiming well at both things, both the sufficient covering of the bodies and the enabling of those who used the pelta, through their lightness, to be wholly nimble.
44.3. The convenience meeting with acceptance through trial, those formerly called from their shields hoplites were then renamed from the pelta peltasts. As for the spear and the sword, he made the change to the opposite; for he increased the spears by half their size, and made the swords almost double. The proof confirming by trial the device of the general, the achievement of the experiment deemed the conception worthy of glory.
44.4. He made the footwear for the soldiers easily loosed and light, those called even to the present day iphicratides from him. He introduced many other things useful for campaigns, about which it would be long to write. The Persian campaign against Egypt, then, having met with great preparation, beyond expectation had a fruitless end.
45.1. In Greece, the cities being disturbed because of the unaccustomed constitution, and many rising up because of the common anarchy, the Lacedaemonians helped those who were establishing oligarchies, while the Athenians allied themselves with those who clung to democracy.
