45.2. For both these cities kept the treaties a little time, but after this, cooperating with their own cities, made war, no longer taking thought of the common concluded peace. Therefore in Zacynthus the people, being harsh and bearing malice toward those who had been masters of the constitution during the supremacy of the Lacedaemonians, banished all . . . These, fleeing to Timotheus the leader of the Athenian fleet, sailed with him and were his allies.
45.3. Setting up this man as cooperator, and being transported to the island by him, they seized a strong stronghold by the sea, which they named Arcadia. Setting out from this, and having Timotheus as helper, they harassed those in the city.
45.4. The Zacynthians asking the Lacedaemonians to help, at first, sending envoys to Athens, they accused Timotheus; but when they saw the people inclining toward the exiles, they constituted a fleet, and manning twenty-five triremes sent out an alliance to the Zacynthians, giving the command to Aristocrates.
46.1. At the same time as these things were being done, some of the people of Corcyra who were friends of the Lacedaemonians, rising up against the people, called upon the Spartans to send a naval force, promising to deliver Corcyra to them. The Lacedaemonians, knowing that Corcyra had a great weight for those who clung to the sea, were eager to become masters of this city.
46.2. Immediately, then, they sent to Corcyra twenty-two triremes, giving the command to Alcidas. They pretended to send this fleet to Sicily, in order that, being received as friends by the Corcyraeans, they might hold the city with the exiles.
46.3. The Corcyraeans, learning the design of the Spartans, carefully guarded the city and sent envoys to Athens for help. The Athenians, voting to help the Corcyraeans and the exiles of the Zacynthians, sent to Zacynthus Ctesicles as general, leading the exiles, and prepared to send a naval force to Corcyra.
46.4. At the same time as these things were being done, in Boeotia the Plataeans, clinging to the alliance with the Athenians, sent for soldiers, having resolved to deliver the city to the Athenians. At this the boeotarchs, being harshly disposed toward the Plataeans and eager to forestall the alliance from the Athenians, immediately led a considerable force against them.
46.5. Coming near the city of the Plataeans, the attack being unexpected, most of the Plataeans, caught in the country by the cavalry, were seized, while the rest, fleeing to the city and being destitute of allies, were compelled to conclude agreements satisfactory to the enemy; for they had to take their movables and depart from the city and no longer set foot in Boeotia.
46.6. After this the Thebans, razing Plataea and plundering Thespiae, which was ill disposed toward them, the Plataeans, fleeing to Athens with children and wives, obtained equal citizenship because of the goodness of the people. And the affairs in Boeotia were in this state.

47.1. The Lacedaemonians, appointing Mnasippus general, sent him out against Corcyra, having sixty-five triremes and fifteen hundred soldiers. He, sailing to the island and taking on the exiles, sailed into the harbour, and mastered four ships, while of the remaining three ships, which fled to the land, these were burned by the Corcyraeans, that they might not become subject to the enemy. He conquered also on land those who had seized a certain hill, and in general set much fear upon the Corcyraeans.
47.2. The Athenians had earlier sent Timotheus the son of Conon to help the Corcyraeans with sixty ships; he, before this alliance, sailing to Thrace and calling many cities to alliance, added thirty triremes;
47.3. but at that time, being late for the alliance of the Corcyraeans, he at first lost his command, the people being harshly disposed toward him; but when he sailed back to Athens, bringing a multitude of envoys of those concluding the alliance and having added thirty triremes, and having well equipped the whole fleet for the war, the people repented and again restored to him the command.
47.4. They constructed besides forty other triremes, so that all became a hundred and thirty; and they made considerable preparations of grain and missiles and the other things useful for war. For the present, choosing Ctesicles as general, they sent him out with five hundred soldiers to help the Corcyraeans.
47.5. He, secretly by night, sailed into Corcyra unobserved by the besiegers; and finding those in the city in faction with one another and managing the war badly, he dissolved the factions, and taking much care of the city made the besieged confident.
47.6. And at first, attacking the besiegers unexpectedly, he slew about two hundred of them; later, a great battle taking place, he both slew Mnasippus and not a few of the others; and at last, shutting up the besiegers in a siege, he met with great praises.
47.7. The war about Corcyra being now almost at an end, the fleet of the Athenians sailed to Corcyra, having as generals Timotheus and Iphicrates. These, being late for the occasions, did nothing else worthy of memory, but falling in with Sicilian triremes, which Dionysius had sent to the Lacedaemonians for alliance, of which Cissides and Crinippus were leaders, they took with all their crews, being nine; and selling the captives as booty, and gathering more than sixty talents, they paid the force.
47.8. At the same time as these things were being done, in Cyprus Nicocles the eunuch treacherously slew Evagoras the king and mastered the kingdom of the Salaminians; and in Italy the Romans, arraying against the Praenestines and conquering, cut down most of those arrayed against them.

48.1. In the archonship at Athens of Asteius the Romans appointed in place of the consuls six military tribunes, Marcus Furius and Lucius Furius, and besides Aulus Postumius and Lucius Lucretius and Marcus Fabius and Lucius Postumius. In this year about the Peloponnese there occurred great earthquakes and incredible inundations of land and cities; for never in the times above had there occurred such sufferings about Greek cities, nor the destruction of cities with all their inhabitants, some divine working having contrived the destruction and ruin of the men.
48.2. The occasion increased the magnitude of the calamity; for the earthquake did not happen by day, in which it was possible for those in danger to help themselves, but the suffering occurring by night, the houses, falling because of the magnitude of the earthquake, were thrown into confusion, and the men, both because of the darkness and the unexpected and paradoxical nature of the situation, were unable to lay hold of safety.
48.3. The greater part, then, caught in the falls of the houses, perished; but when day came on, some leaped out of the houses, and thinking they had escaped the danger, fell into a greater and more paradoxical calamity; for the sea being lifted up to a great height and a high wave being raised, all were overwhelmed and made to disappear together with their fatherlands. This suffering occurred about two cities of Achaea, Helice and Bura, of which Helice happened to have the greatest dignity of the cities in Achaea before the earthquake.
48.4. Concerning the disasters there being great inquiry, the natural philosophers try to refer the causes of such sufferings not to the divine, but to certain natural and necessary circumstances, while those piously disposed toward the divine assign certain plausible causes of what happened, as the calamity having come about through the wrath of the gods upon those who had committed impiety toward the divine; about which we too shall try to write accurately in the particular history.
49.1. In Ionia nine cities were accustomed to make a common assembly, the Panionia, and to sacrifice together ancient and great sacrifices to Poseidon at the place called Mycale in a desert place. Later, wars arising about these places, being unable to hold the Panionia, they transferred the festival to a safe place, which was near Ephesus. Sending envoys to Delphi, they received oracles to take cult-objects from their ancient and ancestral altars from Helice in the country then called Ionian, but now Achaea.
49.2. The Ionians, then, in accordance with the oracle, sent to Achaea those who should take the cult-objects; these, conferring with the common body of the Achaeans, persuaded them to give what was asked. But those dwelling in Helice, having an ancient saying that they would then be in danger when the Ionians sacrificed at the altar of Poseidon, reckoning up the oracle, objected to the Ionians concerning the cult-objects, saying that the precinct was not common to the Achaeans but their own private; and those dwelling in Bura cooperated with them.
49.3. The Achaeans by a common decree consenting, the Ionians sacrificed at the altar of Poseidon in accordance with the oracle, but the people of Helice scattered the property of the Ionians and seized the envoys, and committed impiety toward the divine. In requital of which they say that Poseidon, being wrathful, by the earthquake and the inundation destroyed the impious cities.
49.4. They say that there are clear proofs that the wrath came upon the cities from Poseidon, because this god has been understood to have authority over earthquakes and inundations, and because the Peloponnese is thought in antiquity to have been a dwelling-place of Poseidon, and this country to be reckoned as if sacred to Poseidon, and in sum all the cities in the Peloponnese honour this god most of the immortals.
49.5. Besides these things, the Peloponnese has in its depths great hollows and great gatherings of running waters. For there are in it two rivers manifestly flowing under the earth; for the river about Pheneus, sinking into the earth in former times, disappeared, the caverns underground receiving it, and the one about Stymphelus, sinking into a chasm, is carried for two hundred stades hidden under the earth and comes out by the city of the Argives.
49.6. Besides what has been said, they say that, except for those who committed impiety, no one else fell into the calamity. And concerning the earthquakes and inundations that occurred, we shall be content with what has been said.

50.1. In the archonship at Athens of Alcisthenes the Romans appointed in place of the consuls eight military tribunes, Lucius Valerius and Publius, and besides Gaius Terentius and Lucius Menenius, and besides these Gaius Sulpicius and Titus Papirius and Lucius Aemilius, and among the Eleians the hundred-and-second Olympiad was celebrated, in which Damon the Thurian was victor in the stadion.
50.2. In this year, the Lacedaemonians having held the leadership of Greece for almost five hundred years, the divinity foretokened to them the loss of their rule; for there was seen in the heaven for many nights a great burning torch, named from its shape a fiery beam; and a little later the Spartans, unexpectedly defeated in a great battle, lost their leadership beyond hope.
50.3. Some of the natural philosophers referred the origin of the torch to natural causes, declaring that such apparitions occur of necessity at fixed times, and that about such things the Chaldeans in Babylon and the other astrologers, making clear predictions, hit the mark; and that they do not marvel when such a thing happens, but rather if it does not happen, the things being completed in their own several periods by eternal motions and fixed courses. The torch, at any rate, had such brightness and power of light that it made shadows on the earth like the moon.
50.4. About these times Artaxerxes the King, seeing Greece again disturbed, sent envoys, calling upon them to settle the civil wars and to conclude a common peace according to the agreements which they had previously made. All the Greeks gladly receiving the words, all the cities concluded a common peace except the Thebans; for the Thebans alone, bringing Boeotia under one confederacy, were not received by the Greeks, because it pleased all that the oaths and treaties should be made by city. Therefore, becoming excluded from the treaty as also before, they held Boeotia in their own single confederacy.
50.5. At this the Lacedaemonians, being provoked, resolved to campaign against them with a great force, as common enemies; for they greatly suspected their increase, lest, leading all Boeotia, they should dissolve the leadership of Sparta, having seized an opportunity. For, continually spending time in the gymnasia, they were strong in body, and being by nature warlike they fell behind no Greek nation in valour.
50.6. They had also leaders distinguished in virtue, many others, but three the greatest, Epaminondas and Gorgias, and besides Pelopidas; and the city of the Thebans, through the eminence of their ancestors in the heroic times, was full of spirit and reached out for great deeds. In this year, then, the Lacedaemonians prepared for the war and enrolled forces, some of citizens, some from the allies.

51.1. In the archonship at Athens of Phrasiclides the Romans appointed in place of the consuls eight military tribunes, Publius Manius and Gaius, Erenucius and Gaius Sestus and Tiberius Julius, and besides Lucius Lavinius and Publius Tribonius and Gaius Manlius, and besides these Lucius Antistius. In this year the Thebans, having become excluded from the treaty, were compelled to take up alone the war against the Lacedaemonians; for it was not possible for any city to ally itself, because all had concluded the common peace.
51.2. The Lacedaemonians, the Thebans being isolated, resolved to make war on them and to enslave Thebes. The preparation of the Lacedaemonians being manifest, and the Thebans being destitute of allies, all supposed that they would easily be subdued by the Spartans.
51.3. Therefore those of the Greeks who were well disposed toward the Thebans grieved with them at the expected calamities, while those ill disposed were overjoyed, as the Thebans being immediately about to be enslaved. At last the Lacedaemonians, having prepared a great force, gave it to Cleombrotus the king, and first sent envoys to Thebes, ordering them to leave all the cities in Boeotia independent, to refound Plataea and Thespiae, and to restore the country to those who had earlier been masters.
51.4. The Thebans answering that neither did they themselves meddle in any of the affairs of Laconia, nor was it fitting for the Lacedaemonians to lay hold of the affairs of Boeotia; such answers having been given, the Lacedaemonians immediately sent out Cleombrotus with the force against Thebes; and the allies of the Lacedaemonians were eager for the war, hoping that there would be neither contest nor battle, but that they would master the Boeotians without effort.
52.1. These, then, advancing, when they came to Coronea, encamped and awaited the allies who were late. The Thebans, because of the presence of the enemy, voted to remove their children and wives to Athens, and themselves, choosing Epaminondas as general, entrusted to him the affairs of the war, with six boeotarchs present with him.
52.2. Epaminondas, enrolling in full force the Thebans who were of military age for the battle and the fit men of the other Boeotians, led the force out of Thebes, having in all not more than six thousand.
52.3. At the going out of the city of the soldiers, to many there seemed to appear unfavourable omens for the army. For about the gates a blind herald met Epaminondas and his men, who, recovering runaway slaves, and as was customary, proclaimed announcing that none should lead them out of Thebes nor make them disappear, but should lead them back and bring them safe again.
52.4. The elder of those who heard the herald made an omen of the future, but the younger kept quiet, lest they should seem through cowardice to turn Epaminondas from the campaign. Epaminondas, to those saying they ought to heed the omens, said: "One omen is best, to defend one's fatherland."
52.5. Epaminondas having by this frankness struck dismay into those who were cautious, another omen appeared more troublesome than the former. For the secretary advanced holding a spear with a fillet upon it, and signalled what was commanded by the leaders; a wind arising, it came to pass that the fillet, torn off, was wrapped about a stele standing over a tomb; and there were buried in this place certain Lacedaemonians and Peloponnesians who, having campaigned with Agesilaus, had died.
52.6. Some of the elders, again falling in with this, protested against leading the force forward, the gods manifestly forbidding; but he, answering them nothing, led the army forward, considering that the reckoning on behalf of noble things and the memory of just things were more to be chosen than the present omens.
52.7. Epaminondas, then, having pursued philosophy and prudently using the reasonings from education, at the moment met with blame from many, but later, seeming through his successes to excel in generalship's understanding, became the cause of the greatest goods to his fatherland. For immediately leading the force forward, and forestalling the seizure of the narrows about Coronea, he encamped.

53.1. Cleombrotus, learning that the enemy had forestalled him in seizing the passes, gave up making his way through there, but marching through Phocis, and going through the coast road, which was difficult, he invaded Boeotia without danger; and along the way mastering certain small fortified towns, he gained possession of ten triremes.
53.2. After this, coming to the place called Leuctra, he encamped and refreshed the soldiers from the march. The Boeotians, advancing against the enemy, when they drew near them and, crossing certain hills, suddenly perceived the Lacedaemonians occupying the whole Leuctrian plain, were struck with dismay seeing the magnitude of the force.
53.3. The boeotarchs taking counsel together and deliberating whether they ought to remain and fight it out against a force many times larger, or, making their withdrawal, constitute the battle in commanding positions, the opinions of the leaders happened to be equal. For there being six boeotarchs, three thought they ought to lead the force away, and three to remain and fight it out, among whom Epaminondas too was counted. Great and hard-to-decide being the perplexity, a seventh boeotarch came, whom Epaminondas, persuading to become of one vote with him, had the advantage in the opinion. The contest for the whole, then, was in this manner ratified.
53.4. Epaminondas, seeing the soldiers superstitious because of the omens that had occurred, was ambitious by his own device and generalship to change the precautions of the multitude. Therefore, certain men having lately come from Thebes, he persuaded them to say that the arms about the temple of Heracles had unexpectedly become invisible, and that word had spread in Thebes that the ancient heroes had taken them up and gone away to help the Boeotians. He set up another as having lately come up from Trophonius and saying that the god had ordered them, when they conquered at Leuctra, to establish a contest with crowns for Zeus the King; from which indeed the Boeotians hold this festival at Lebadea.
54.1. Leandrias the Spartan cooperated in this device, having fled from Lacedaemon and at that time campaigning with the Thebans. This man, brought forward in the assembly, declared that there was an ancient saying among the Spartans that they would then lose their leadership when at Leuctra they should be defeated by the Thebans.
54.2. There came also to Epaminondas certain native oracle-interpreters, saying that about the tomb of the daughters of Leuctrus and Scedasus the Lacedaemonians must fall into a great calamity for some such causes as these.
54.3. There was a Leuctrus, from whom this plain got its name. The daughters of this man and likewise the maidens of a certain Scedasus envoys of the Lacedaemonians outraged; and they, having been outraged, not bearing the misfortune, cursing the fatherland that had sent the outragers, ended their lives by their own hand.
54.4. Many other such things being told, and Epaminondas having gathered an assembly and exhorted the soldiers with appropriate speeches to the contest, all changed their opinions, and were released from their superstition, and became confident in their souls for the battle.
54.5. There came also at this time an alliance to the Thebans from the Thessalians, foot fifteen hundred and horse five hundred, of whom Jason was leader. He persuaded both the Boeotians and the Lacedaemonians to make a truce and to be on their guard against the unaccountable turns of fortune.
54.6. The truce being made, Cleombrotus broke camp with the force from Boeotia, and there met him another great force of Lacedaemonians and the allies, led by Archidamus the son of Agesilaus. For the Spartans, observing the readiness of the Boeotians, and being on their guard against the boldness and desperation, had sent out the second force, that by the multitude of those fighting they might overcome the daring of the enemy.
54.7. The forces having come together into one, the Lacedaemonians supposed it to be shameful to fear the valours of the Boeotians. Therefore, holding the truce as nothing, with much eagerness they came back to Leuctra. The Boeotians being also ready for battle, both sides drew up their forces.

55.1. Among the Lacedaemonians the leaders descended from Heracles were stationed on the wings, Cleombrotus the king and Archidamus the son of Agesilaus the king; among the Boeotians Epaminondas, using a peculiar and extraordinary order, through his own generalship won the renowned victory.
55.2. For choosing from the whole force the best, he stationed them on the one part, with whom he himself also was about to fight it out; the weakest he stationed on the other wing and ordered them to avoid battle and, at the onset of the enemy, to withdraw little by little. Therefore, making the phalanx oblique, he decided to decide the battle by the wing that had the chosen men.
55.3. When the trumpets on both sides signalled the battle-cry, and at the first onset the forces raised the war-shout together, the Lacedaemonians with both wings advanced, having made the shape of the phalanx crescent-like, while the Boeotians with the one wing withdrew, but with the other at a run engaged the enemy.
55.4. When they came to close quarters with one another, at first both sides fighting ardently, the battle was even; but after this, the men of Epaminondas, having the advantage both through their valour and the density of the formation, many of the Peloponnesians were slain. For they did not endure to bear the weight of the bravery of the chosen men, but of those who withstood, some fell, others were wounded, receiving all the blows in front.
55.5. So long, then, as Cleombrotus the king of the Lacedaemonians lived, having many who locked shields with him and eagerly died before him, the turn of the victory was unclear; but when this man, enduring every danger, was unable to force those who withstood, but fighting heroically and falling in with many wounds died, then, a concourse occurring about the body, a multitude of corpses was heaped up.
56.1. There being anarchy about the wing, the men of Epaminondas, pressing heavily upon the Lacedaemonians, at first by force pushed the enemy a little from their position, while the Lacedaemonians, fighting brilliantly about the king, became masters of the body, but had not strength to attain the victory.
56.2. The chosen men surpassing in bravery, and the virtue and exhortation of Epaminondas contributing much, the Lacedaemonians with difficulty were forced back; at first, withdrawing, they did not break their formation, but at last, many being slain and the commanding leader having died, there occurred a complete rout of the army.
56.3. The men of Epaminondas, pressing upon the fleeing and cutting down many of the enemy, carried off a most notable victory. For having engaged with the best of the Greeks, and with few unexpectedly prevailing over many times their number, they acquired a great reputation for valour. The greatest praises were given to the general Epaminondas, who by his own valour especially and generalship's understanding had overcome the unconquered leaders of Greece.
56.4. There fell in the battle of the Lacedaemonians not fewer than four thousand, and of the Boeotians about three hundred. After this, concerning the taking up of the dead and the departure of the Lacedaemonians to the Peloponnese, they made a truce. And the things that occurred about the battle at Leuctra had such an end.
57.1. The annual period having passed, at Athens the archon was Dysnicetus, and at Rome four military tribunes were appointed in place of the consuls, Quintus Servilius and Lucius Furius, and besides Gaius Licinius and Publius Caelius. In this year the Thebans, campaigning against Orchomenus with a great force, attempted to enslave the city, but Epaminondas advising that those who reach out for the leadership of the Greeks ought to preserve by humanity the things accomplished by valour, they changed their mind. Therefore they ranged the Orchomenians among the allied country, and after this, making the Phocians and Aetolians and Locrians friends, they made their return into Boeotia.
57.2. Jason the tyrant of Pherae, ever increasing more, campaigned into Locris, and Heraclea in Trachis, taking it through betrayal, he made desolate, and gave the country to the Oetaeans and Malians; after this, breaking camp to Perrhaebia, of the cities some he brought over by humane speeches, others he mastered by force. His dominion quickly being strengthened, those dwelling in Thessaly suspected his increase and greed.
57.3. At the same time as these things were being done, in the city of the Argives there occurred faction and so great a slaughter as is recorded never to have occurred among any others of the Greeks. This revolution was called among the Greeks the clubbing, from the manner of the death receiving this name.
58.1. The faction occurred for some such causes as these. The city of the Argives being a democracy and certain demagogues provoking the multitude against those superior in power and reputation, those slandered, banding together, resolved to overthrow the democracy.
58.2. Some of those thought to be cooperators being tortured, the rest, fearing the punishment from the tortures, removed themselves from life; but one in the tortures confessing and receiving a pledge, the informer accused thirty of the most notable, and the people, not having tested accurately all who had been slandered, slew them and confiscated their properties.
58.3. Many others being under suspicion, and the demagogues supporting with false slanders, the multitude was so far enraged that of all the accused, being many and very wealthy, they condemned to death. More than twelve hundred of the powerful men being slain, the people did not even spare the demagogues themselves.
58.4. For because of the magnitude of the calamity the demagogues, fearing lest something unaccountable befall them, desisted from the accusation, and the crowds, thinking themselves abandoned by them, and on this account provoked, slew all the demagogues. These, then, as if some divinity took vengeance, met with the fitting punishment, and the people, ceasing from their frenzy, returned to their former understanding.

59.1. About the same times Lycomedes the Tegeate persuaded the Arcadians to be ranged into one confederacy and to have a common assembly composed of ten thousand men, and that these should have authority to deliberate about war and peace.
59.2. A great faction occurring among the Arcadians, and those at variance being decided by arms, many were slain, and more than fourteen hundred fled, some to Sparta, others to Pallantium.
59.3. These, then, given up by the Pallantians, were slaughtered by the victors; and those who fled to Sparta persuaded the Lacedaemonians to campaign into Arcadia.
59.4. Therefore Agesilaus the king, with a force and the exiles, invaded the country of the Tegeates, because these seemed to have been the cause of the faction and the flight. Ravaging the country and making assaults on the city, he struck dismay into those of the Arcadians who acted against him.
60.1. At the same time as these things were being done, Jason the tyrant of Pherae, distinguished in generalship's understanding and having brought many of the neighbours into alliance, persuaded the Thessalians to lay claim to the leadership of the Greeks; for this, as a kind of prize of valour, lay before those able to dispute it.
60.2. For it came to pass that the Lacedaemonians had fallen into a great calamity at Leuctra, that the Athenians clung only to the rule by sea, that the Thebans were not worthy of the first place, and that the Argives had been humbled because of factions and civil slaughters. Therefore the Thessalians, setting up Jason as leader of the whole, entrusted to him the affairs of the war. Jason, taking over the leadership, brought over certain of the neighbouring peoples and made an alliance with Amyntas the king of the Macedonians.
60.3. Something peculiar occurred in this year; for of those in positions of power three died about the same time. Amyntas the son of Arrhidaeus, reigning over Macedonia, died, having ruled twenty-four years, leaving three sons, Alexander and Perdiccas and Philip; his son Alexander succeeded to the kingdom and ruled a year.
60.4. Likewise also Agesipolis the king of the Lacedaemonians passed away, having ruled a year, and his brother Cleomenes, succeeding to the rule, reigned thirty-four years.
60.5. Third, Jason the Pheraean, chosen leader of Thessaly, and seeming to rule his subjects fairly, was treacherously slain, as Ephorus has written, by certain seven young men who conspired for the sake of glory, but as some write, by Polydorus his brother. This man too, succeeding to the dominion, ruled a year.
60.6. Duris the Samian the historian made the beginning of his Greek history from here. These things, then, were done in this year.

61.1. In the archonship at Athens of Lysistratus, among the Romans there occurred faction, some thinking they ought to choose consuls, others military tribunes. For some time, then, anarchy held the faction, but after this it was resolved to choose six military tribunes; and there were appointed Lucius Aemilius and Gaius Verginius and Servius Sulpicius, and besides these Lucius Quinctius and Gaius Cornelius, and besides Gaius Valerius.
61.2. In this year Polydorus the Pheraean, who had ruled the Thessalians, was slain by Alexander his nephew with poison, having been invited to drink; and his nephew Alexander, succeeding to the dominion, ruled eleven years. This man, having acquired the dominion lawlessly and violently, managed the affairs of his rule in accordance with this choice. For while the rulers before him dealt fairly with the multitude, and on this account were loved, this man, ruling violently and harshly, was hated.
61.3. Therefore, fearing his lawlessness, certain of the Larissaeans, those called from their nobility Aleuadae, agreed with one another to overthrow the dominion. Departing from Larissa into Macedonia, they persuaded Alexander the king to help overthrow the tyrant.
61.4. While these were occupied about this, Alexander the Pheraean, learning of the preparation against himself, enrolled the men fit for the campaign, planning to constitute the battle in Macedonia. But the king of the Macedonians, having with him the exiles from Larissa, forestalling the enemy, came with his force to Larissa; brought inside the walls by the Larissaeans, he mastered the city except for the citadel.
61.5. After this he both took the citadel by siege and, bringing over the city Crannon, agreed to give back the cities to the Thessalians; but despising the engagement, and bringing in considerable garrisons, he himself held the cities. The Pheraean Alexander, both pursued and struck with dismay, returned to Pherae. And the affairs in Thessaly were in this state.
62.1. In the Peloponnese the Lacedaemonians sent Polytropus as general into Arcadia, having a thousand citizen hoplites and five hundred exiles of the Argives and Boeotians. He, coming to Arcadian Orchomenus, guarded this city, which was favourably disposed toward the Spartans.
62.2. Lycomedes the Mantinean, being general of the Arcadians, taking the men called the chosen, being five thousand, came to Orchomenus. The Lacedaemonians leading the force out of the city, a fierce battle took place, in which both the general of the Lacedaemonians was slain and of the others about two hundred; the rest were pursued together into the city.
62.3. The Arcadians, although they had conquered, nevertheless were on their guard against the weight of Sparta, and did not suppose they would be able by themselves to fight the war against the Lacedaemonians. Therefore, taking on the Argives and Eleians, at first they sent envoys to Athens, asking them to make an alliance against the Spartans; but when no one heeded them, sending an embassy to the Thebans they persuaded them to conclude an alliance against the Lacedaemonians.
62.4. Immediately, then, the Boeotians led out the force, taking on as allies both Locrians and Phocians. These, then, advanced against the Peloponnese, Epaminondas and Pelopidas being boeotarchs; for to these the other boeotarchs had willingly yielded the generalship, because of the understanding and valour of the men.
62.5. When they came to Arcadia, there came to them in full force both the Arcadians and Eleians and Argives and all the other allies. More than fifty thousand being gathered, their leaders, taking counsel together, resolved to march against Sparta itself and to ravage all Laconia.

63.1. The Lacedaemonians, having lost many of their young men in the calamity at Leuctra, and having lost not a few in the other defeats, and in sum being shut up by fortune into few citizen-soldiers, and besides this their allies, some having revolted, some for like causes being short of men, fell into great helplessness. Therefore they were compelled to flee for refuge to the aid of the Athenians, upon whom in former times they had set thirty tyrants, whom they had prevented from rebuilding the walls of their city, and whom they had attempted, by utterly destroying the city, to make Attica a sheep-pasture.
63.2. But indeed nothing is stronger than necessity and fortune, by which the Lacedaemonians were forced to beg of their bitterest enemies. Nevertheless they were not deceived of their hopes. For the people of the Athenians, being magnanimous and humane, were not struck with dismay at the strength of the Thebans, but voted to help the Lacedaemonians, who were in danger of being enslaved, in full force. And at once, appointing Iphicrates general, they sent out the young men on the same day, being twelve thousand. Iphicrates, then, having his soldiers eager, advanced with the force in haste.
63.3. The Lacedaemonians, the enemy encamping on the borders of Laconia, themselves also in full force making their going out from Sparta, advanced against their opponents, humbled in the forces of their soldiers, but confident in the virtues of their souls.
63.4. The men of Epaminondas, seeing the country of the Lacedaemonians hard to invade, did not think it of advantage to make the invasion in a single such great force, but dividing themselves into four parts decided to make the onset at several places.
64.1. The first part, that of the Boeotians, made its march in the middle against the city called Sellasia, and made those dwelling there revolt from the Lacedaemonians.
64.2. The Argives, invading by the borders of the Tegeatid country, joined battle with those guarding the passes, and both slew the leader of the garrison, Alexander the Spartan, and slew of the others about two hundred, among whom were also the exiles of the Boeotians.
64.3. The third part, composed of the Arcadians and having the most soldiers, invaded the country called the Sciritis, which Ischolas, a man distinguished in valour and understanding, was guarding with many soldiers. This man, of the most notable soldiers, accomplished a heroic deed worthy of memory.
64.4. For seeing that because of the multitude of the enemy all who joined battle would be slain, he judged it unworthy of Sparta to leave the post in the passes, but that to save the soldiers would be useful to the fatherland; therefore, unexpectedly he provided for both, and zealously imitated the valour of King Leonidas at Thermopylae of old.
64.5. For having picked out the young men, these he sent to Sparta, to be useful to her who was in danger about the whole; while he himself, with the elders, guarding the post and slaying many of the enemy, surrounded by the Arcadians, was slain with all his men.
64.6. The Eleians, having the fourth part, and going through other regions that were open, came to Hellasia; for to this place all had been ordered to come. The whole force being gathered at Hellasia, they advanced against Sparta itself, ravaging at the same time and burning the country.
65.1. The Lacedaemonians, having kept Laconia unravaged for five hundred years, then seeing it laid waste by the enemy, did not endure, but, rushing forward in their wrath, leaped out of the city; being prevented by the elders from advancing too far from their fatherland, lest someone attack, they were persuaded to keep quiet and to provide safety for the city.
65.2. The men of Epaminondas coming down through Taygetus to the Eurotas, and crossing the river, which was violent in its stream in the winter season, the Lacedaemonians, seeing the force of their opponents thrown into confusion because of the difficulty of the crossing, took a fit opportunity for an attack, and leaving the women and children, and besides the aged, in the city to guard Sparta, they themselves, having arrayed the young men in full force, poured out against the enemy, and falling suddenly upon those crossing, made much slaughter.
65.3. The Boeotians and Arcadians defending and surrounding their opponents by their multitude, the Spartans, having slain many, returned to the city, having manifestly displayed their own bravery.
65.4. After this, the men of Epaminondas attacking the city with the whole force strikingly, the Spartans, having as helper the strength of the places, slew many of those who rashly forced their way; and at last the besiegers, bringing in every zeal, at first hoped to master Sparta by force; but when of those who forced their way some died and some were wounded, the men of Epaminondas recalled the soldiers by the trumpet, and themselves, coming up to the city, challenged the Spartans to battle, or ordered them to agree that they were inferior to the enemy.
65.5. The Spartans answering that, taking a fit opportunity, they would fight it out for the whole, they departed from the city. Having ravaged all Laconia and gathered a countless multitude of booty, they withdrew to Arcadia.
65.6. After this the Athenians, being late for the occasions, returned to Attica, having done nothing worthy of memory; but to the Lacedaemonians there came from the allies four thousand soldiers to help. Besides these, adding the Helots lately freed, a thousand, and of the Boeotian exiles two hundred, and besides sending for not a few from the nearby cities, they prepared a force a match for the enemy. Holding this together in mass and exercising it, they ever took more courage and prepared for the contest about the whole.

66.1. Epaminondas, being by nature of great designs and reaching out for eternal glory, advised the Arcadians and the other allies to refound Messene, which had been many years desolate by the Lacedaemonians and had a favourable position against Sparta. All agreeing, he sought out the survivors of the Messenians, and enrolling such of the others as wished into the citizenship, he refounded Messene, making many its inhabitants. Allotting the country to them and rebuilding it, he restored a notable Greek city, and met with great acceptance among all men.
66.2. I think it not foreign, Messene having often been taken and razed, to run over from the beginning the things about it as in a summary. In antiquity, then, the descendants of Neleus and Nestor held it until the Trojan times, and after this Orestes the son of Agamemnon and his descendants until the return of the Heracleidae, and from this Cresphontes received the Messenian portion, and his descendants reigned over it for a time; later, the descendants of Cresphontes losing the kingdom, the Lacedaemonians became masters of it.
66.3. After this, Teleclus the king of the Lacedaemonians having died in a contest, the Messenians were subdued by the Lacedaemonians. This war they say lasted twenty years, the Lacedaemonians having sworn not to return to Sparta unless they took Messene. At that time it came to pass that those named the Partheniae were born and founded the city of the Tarentines. Later, the Messenians being slaves to the Lacedaemonians, Aristomenes persuaded the Messenians to revolt from the Spartans, and he did many evils to the Spartans, at which time also Tyrtaeus the poet was given by the Athenians as leader to the Spartans.
66.4. Some say that Aristomenes lived during the twenty-year war. Their last war occurred when a great earthquake had taken place; and Sparta being almost entirely thrown into confusion and becoming destitute of men, the survivors of the Messenians settled Ithome with the Helots who had revolted with them, Messene having been made desolate for many years.
66.5. Being unfortunate in all the wars, at last, becoming desolate, they settled at Naupactus, the Athenians having given them this city for a dwelling. And some of them were cast out into Cephallenia, and some settled in Sicily Messene, named from them.
66.6. And lastly, in the times in question, the Thebans, Epaminondas having persuaded them and gathered the Messenians from everywhere, settled Messene and restored to them their ancient country. Concerning Messene, then, so many and so great changes came to pass.
67.1. The Thebans, having accomplished all the aforesaid things in eighty-five days, and leaving a considerable guard of Messene, returned home. The Lacedaemonians, having unexpectedly got rid of the enemy, sent as envoys to Athens the most notable of the Spartans, and made the agreements about the leadership, so that the Athenians should rule the sea and the Lacedaemonians the land, and after this in both cities they made the leaderships common.
67.2. The Arcadians, providing Lycomedes as general, and giving him the men called the chosen, being five thousand, campaigned against Pellene in Laconia, and mastering the city by force slew the Lacedaemonian guards left in it, being more than three hundred, and enslaving the city and ravaging the country returned home, forestalling the help from the Lacedaemonians.
67.3. The Boeotians, the Thessalians sending for them for the freeing of the cities and the overthrow of the tyranny of Alexander of Pherae, sent out Pelopidas with a force into Thessaly, giving him instructions to manage the affairs in Thessaly for the advantage of the Boeotians.
67.4. He, coming to Larissa and finding the citadel garrisoned by Alexander the Macedonian, took it over, and going into Macedonia and making an alliance with Alexander the king of the Macedonians, received from him as a hostage his brother Philip, whom he sent to Thebes. Having managed the affairs in Thessaly as seemed to him advantageous to the Boeotians, he returned home.

68.1. These things being done, the Arcadians and Argives and Eleians, conspiring together, resolved to campaign against the Lacedaemonians, and sending an embassy to the Boeotians persuaded them to share in the war. They, appointing Epaminondas leader with other boeotarchs, sent out soldiers, seven thousand foot and six hundred horse. The Athenians, learning that the Boeotian army was passing into the Peloponnese, sent out a force and as general over it Chabrias.
68.2. He, coming to Corinth and taking on soldiers also from the Megarians and Pellenians, and besides Corinthians, constituted an army of ten thousand men; after this, the Lacedaemonians and the other allies coming to Corinth, there were gathered in all not fewer than twenty thousand.
68.3. It seemed best to them, then, to fortify the passes and to prevent the Boeotians from invading the Peloponnese. Beginning from Cenchreae as far as Lechaeum, they cut off the place with palisades and deep trenches; the works being quickly completed both because of the multitude of hands and the eagerness of the men, they forestalled the Boeotians, having fortified every place.
68.4. Epaminondas, coming with the force, examined it, and perceiving that the place where the Lacedaemonians were keeping guard was the easiest to approach, at first challenged the enemy to battle, being almost three times their number in multitude; but when no one dared to come out beyond the fortification, but all defended from the palisade, he brought force against the enemy.
68.5. At every place, then, there were fierce assaults, but most of all against the Lacedaemonians, the places being easy of approach and hard to guard. A great rivalry occurring on both sides, Epaminondas, having with him the best of the Thebans, with difficulty forced the Lacedaemonians; and breaking through their guard and leading the force across, he passed into the Peloponnese, having accomplished a deed in no way inferior to those previously achieved.
69.1. Immediately marching against Troezen and Epidaurus, he ravaged the country, but was unable to master the cities because they had considerable garrisons; Sicyon, however, and Phlius and certain other cities, striking them with dismay, he brought over. Campaigning against Corinth, and the Corinthians coming out, conquering them in battle, he pursued them within the walls; but the Boeotians, lifted up by their success, and certain of them rashly daring to force their way through the gate into the city, the Corinthians, fearing, turned to their houses, while Chabrias the general of the Athenians, prudently and at the same time confidently withstanding, both cast them out of the city and laid low many of the Boeotians.
69.2. A rivalry arising, the Boeotians, arraying the whole force, advanced against Corinth strikingly, and Chabrias, taking up the Athenians, advanced out of the city, and seizing the commanding positions withstood the onset of the enemy.
69.3. The Boeotians, then, trusting in the strength of their bodies and the experience from continual wars, hoped by force to master the Athenians, but the men of Chabrias, fighting from commanding positions and many things being supplied from the city, some of those who forced their way they slew, others they wounded.
69.4. The Boeotians, having suffered much, but being able to accomplish nothing, made their withdrawal. Chabrias, then, admired for valour and generalship's understanding, in this manner got rid of the enemy.
70.1. From Sicily Celts and Iberians, two thousand, sailed to Corinth, sent out by Dionysius the tyrant to ally with the Lacedaemonians, having received their pay for five months. The Greeks, wishing to make trial of them, led them forward, and in the encounters and battles, they behaving bravely, many both of the Boeotians and of the allies were slain by them. Therefore, seeming to excel in dexterity and valour and having rendered many services, and being honoured by the Lacedaemonians, at the end of the summer they were sent out to Sicily.

70.2. After this Philiscus, sent out by Artaxerxes the King, sailed to Greece, calling on the Greeks to settle their wars and to conclude a common peace. All the others gladly obeyed, but the Thebans, in accordance with their own principle bringing all Boeotia under one confederacy, were not admitted. The common peace being given up, Philiscus, leaving for the Lacedaemonians two thousand chosen mercenaries having received their pay, departed to Asia.
70.3. At the same time as these things were being done, Euphron the Sicyonian, distinguished in boldness and desperation, taking the Argives as cooperators, attempted a tyranny. Mastering his undertaking, he banished forty of the wealthiest of the Sicyonians, confiscating their properties, and becoming master of much money he gathered mercenaries and ruled the city.
71.1. In the archonship at Athens of Nausigenes, at Rome four military tribunes were appointed in place of the consuls, Lucius Papirius, Lucius Menenius, Servius Cornelius, Servius Sulpicius, and among the Eleians the hundred-and-third Olympiad was celebrated, in which Pythostratus the Athenian was victor in the stadion. In this year Ptolemy the Alorite, the son of Amyntas, treacherously slew Alexander his brother, and reigned over Macedonia three years.
71.2. In Boeotia Pelopidas, being a rival of Epaminondas in reputation in war, and seeing that he had advantageously arranged the affairs about the Peloponnese for the Boeotians, was eager to bring over the affairs outside the Peloponnese to the Thebans through himself. Taking Ismenias, a man his own friend and admired for virtue, he went to Thessaly. Coming to Alexander the tyrant of Pherae, he was unaccountably arrested together with Ismenias and given over to prison.
71.3. The Thebans being provoked at what had been done, and quickly sending out into Thessaly eight thousand hoplites and six hundred horse, Alexander, fearing, sent envoys to Athens about an alliance. To him immediately the people sent thirty ships and a thousand soldiers, of whom Autocles was general.
71.4. While this man was sailing round Euboea, the Thebans came to Thessaly. Alexander having gathered an infantry force and having many times more horse than the Boeotians, at first the Boeotians decided to settle the war by battle, having the Thessalians as cooperators; but when these abandoned them, and the Athenians and certain other allies came to Alexander, and food and drink and all else failed the Boeotians, the boeotarchs resolved to make their return home.
71.5. As they broke camp, and the march being through a plain country, Alexander followed with many horsemen and attacked those in the rearguard. Of the Boeotians some, being shot down continually, died, others fell in with wounds, and at last, being allowed neither to remain nor to advance, they fell into great helplessness, since the necessaries also were scarce.
71.6. They now despairing of their safety, Epaminondas, being a private man at that time, was appointed general by the soldiers. Immediately, picking out the light-armed and the horsemen, these he himself took, and being stationed in the rearguard, through these he held off the pursuing enemy and provided much safety for the hoplites leading the way; and making battles by turning back and using a skilful order, he saved the army.
71.7. Ever increasing his own good repute through his successes, he met with great acceptance both among the citizens and the allies. The Thebans, condemning those who had then been boeotarchs, fined them a sum of money.
72.1. The cause being sought, how such a man, being a private person, campaigned with those sent to Thessaly, the proper account of the explanation must be given. In the battle about Corinth Epaminondas, breaking through the guard of the Lacedaemonians on the outwork, and being able to slay many of the enemy, was content with the advantage and desisted from further battle.
72.2. A sufficient suspicion arising about him, as having spared the Lacedaemonians for the sake of a private favour, those who envied his reputation took an opportunity for a plausible slander. Bringing therefore against him a charge of treason, the multitude, provoked, removed him from the boeotarchy, and making him a private man sent him out with the others. But when by the outcomes he wiped out the slanders against himself, then the people restored him to his former good repute.
72.3. A little time later, a great battle occurred for the Lacedaemonians against the Arcadians, in which the Lacedaemonians conspicuously conquered. For after the defeat at Leuctra this was the first unexpected good fortune for them; for there fell of the Arcadians above ten thousand, and of the Lacedaemonians none. The priestesses of Dodona had foretold to them that this war would be tearless for the Lacedaemonians.
72.4. After the battle the Arcadians, fearing the invasions of the Lacedaemonians, founded on a certain strategic place the city named Megalopolis (the Great City), throwing together into it twenty villages of the Arcadians called Maenalians and Parrasians. And the affairs of the Greeks were in this state.

73.1. In Sicily Dionysius the tyrant, having considerable forces, and seeing the Carthaginians not well disposed toward the war both because of the pestilential disease that had occurred among them and the revolt of the Libyans, resolved to campaign against them. Not having a notable pretext for the quarrel, he pretended that the Phoenicians in his dominion had set foot upon the country under him.
73.2. Having prepared thirty thousand foot, three thousand horse, three hundred triremes, and the supply fitting for this force, he invaded the country under the Carthaginians. He immediately brought over Selinus and Entella, and ravaging the whole country and becoming master of the city of the Erycini, he besieged Lilybaeum; but there being many soldiers in it, he raised the siege.
73.3. Hearing that the dockyards of the Carthaginians had been burned, and thinking that their whole fleet had been destroyed, he was contemptuous, and of his own triremes he sent the best hundred and thirty to the harbour of the Erycini, and the rest he sent all to Syracuse.
73.4. The Carthaginians, unexpectedly manning two hundred ships, sailed against those moored in the harbour of the Erycini; the attack being unexpected, they carried off most of the triremes. After this, winter setting in, making a truce, they parted to their own cities, each side.
73.5. A little time later Dionysius, falling into sickness, died, having ruled thirty-eight years; and his son Dionysius, succeeding to the rule, was tyrant twelve years.
74.1. It is not foreign to the present history to relate both the causes of his death and the things that befell this ruler about the end of his life. Dionysius, then, having produced a tragedy at Athens at the Lenaea and won, one of those who sang in the chorus, supposing he would be brilliantly honoured if he were the first to announce the victory, sailed to Corinth. Finding there a ship sailing to Sicily and transferring to it, he had favouring winds, and sailing to Syracuse quickly announced the victory to the tyrant.
74.2. Dionysius honoured this man, and himself became overjoyed, and sacrificing thank-offerings to the gods held drinking-parties and great feasts. Entertaining his friends brilliantly, and at the drinking giving himself rather ambitiously to drunkenness, he fell into a more severe sickness because of the quantity of the liquids he had drunk down.
74.3. Having from the gods an oracle that he would die when he should prevail over his betters, he referred the oracle to the Carthaginians, supposing them to be his betters. Therefore, having often made war on them, he was accustomed in his victories to withdraw and willingly to be defeated, that he might not seem to have become better than the stronger.
74.4. Nevertheless he was unable by his cunning to outwit the necessity from fate, but being a bad poet and judged at Athens he conquered the better poets. Reasonably, then, according to the oracle, through prevailing over his betters he had the end of his life follow.
74.5. Dionysius the younger, succeeding to the tyranny, first gathering the multitude into an assembly, exhorted them with appropriate speeches to keep their hereditary goodwill toward him, then, having buried his father magnificently in the citadel by the gates called the Royal, he secured the affairs of his rule.

75.1. In the archonship at Athens of Polyzelus, in Rome there occurred anarchy because of certain political factions, and in Greece Alexander the tyrant of Pherae in Thessaly, having brought certain charges against the city of the Scotussaeans, called them to an assembly, and surrounding them with all his mercenaries slaughtered them, and casting the bodies of the dead into the trench before the walls, plundered the city.
75.2. Epaminondas the Theban, invading the Peloponnese with a force, brought over the Achaeans and certain other cities, and freed Dyme and Naupactus and Calydon, which was garrisoned by the Achaeans. The Boeotians campaigned also into Thessaly, and recovered Pelopidas from Alexander the tyrant of Pherae.
75.3. The Phliasians being warred upon by the Argives, Chares, sent by the Athenians as general with a force, helped; conquering the Argives in two battles and securing safety for the Phliasians, he returned to Athens.
76.1. The annual period having passed, at Athens the archon was Cephisodorus, and at Rome the people appointed four military tribunes in place of the consuls, Lucius Furius, Paulus Manlius, Servius Sulpicius, Servius Cornelius. In this year Themison the tyrant of Eretria seized Oropus. This city, being the Athenians', he lost unaccountably; for when the Athenians campaigned against him and far surpassed him in forces, the Thebans, coming to his aid and receiving the city as a trust, did not give it back.
76.2. At the same time as these things were being done, the Coans removed to the city now inhabited and constructed it considerable; for a multitude of men was gathered into it, and costly walls were built and a considerable harbour. From these times it ever increased more both in public revenues and in the wealth of private persons, and in sum became a rival to the foremost cities.
76.3. At the same time as these things were being done, the King of the Persians, sending envoys, persuaded the Greeks to settle their wars and to conclude a common peace with one another. Therefore the war called both the Laconian and the Boeotian was dissolved, having lasted more than five years, taking its beginning from the events at Leuctra.
76.4. There existed at these times men worthy of memory for education, Isocrates the orator and his pupils, and Aristotle the philosopher, and besides Anaximenes of Lampsacus and Plato the Athenian, and besides, of the Pythagorean philosophers the last, and Xenophon who wrote the histories, being in extreme old age; for he mentions the death of Epaminondas which occurred a little time later; and Aristippus and Antisthenes, and besides these Aeschines of Sphettus the Socratic.

77.1. In the archonship at Athens of Chion, at Rome military tribunes were appointed in place of the consuls, Quintus Servilius and Gaius Vetorius and Aulus Cornelius, and besides these Marcus Cornelius and Marcus Fabius. In this year, there being peace throughout all Greece, again beginnings of wars arose for certain of the cities and an unaccountable innovation of new affairs. For the exiles of the Arcadians, setting out from Elis, seized in the country called Triphylia a strong stronghold, which is named Lasion.
77.2. For many years the Arcadians and Eleians had disputed about Triphylia, and according to the superiority of each in the changes they alternately mastered the country; but at the times in question, the Arcadians holding Triphylia, the Eleians, with the pretext of the exiles, took it away from the Arcadians.
77.3. Therefore the Arcadians, being provoked, at first, sending out envoys, demanded back the stronghold; but when no one heeded them, they sent for an alliance from the Athenians and with this campaigned against Lasion. The Eleians coming to the aid of the exiles, a battle occurred near Lasion, and the Arcadians being many times more, the Eleians were defeated and lost more than two hundred soldiers.
77.4. This being the beginning of the war, it came to pass that the difference advanced further for the Arcadians and the Eleians; for immediately the Arcadians, lifted up by their advantage, campaigned against Elis, and took the cities Margana and Cronion, and besides Cyparissia and Coryphasium.
77.5. At the same time as these things were being done, in Macedonia Ptolemy the Alorite was treacherously slain by his brother Perdiccas, having reigned three years; and Perdiccas, succeeding to the rule, reigned over Macedonia five years.
78.1. In the archonship at Athens of Timocrates, at Rome three military tribunes were appointed in place of the consuls, Titus Quinctius and Servius Cornelius and Servius Sulpicius, and the Olympiad was celebrated by the Pisatans and Arcadians, the hundred-and-fourth, in which Phocides the Athenian was victor in the stadion.
78.2. In this year the Pisatans, renewing the ancient dignity of their fatherland and using certain mythical and ancient proofs, declared that the conduct of the Olympic festival belonged to them. Judging the present occasion fit to dispute the contest, they made an alliance with the Arcadians, who were enemies of the Eleians; and taking these as fellow-fighters, they campaigned against the Eleians who were just then holding the contest.
78.3. The Eleians withstanding in full force, a fierce battle took place, the Greeks present at the festival, crowned and at leisure, watching the battle without danger and signalling the bravery on each side. At last the Pisatans, conquering, held the contest, and this Olympiad the Eleians did not afterward record, because it seemed to have been conducted by force and unjustly.
78.4. At the same time as these things were being done, Epaminondas the Theban, having the greatest dignity of the citizens, an assembly being gathered, discoursed to the citizens, urging them to lay hold of the leadership by sea. Setting forth a speech long pondered, he showed this undertaking to be both advantageous and possible, both bringing forward other things and that for those who prevail on land it is easy to acquire the rule of the sea; for the Athenians too, in the war against Xerxes, manning two hundred ships of their own, had been subject to the Lacedaemonians who furnished ten. Having appropriately discoursed many other things toward this purpose, he persuaded the Thebans to lay hold of the rule by sea.

79.1. Immediately, then, the people voted to build a hundred triremes and dockyards equal in number to these, and to urge the Rhodians and Chians and Byzantines to help the undertakings. He himself, sent out with a force to the aforesaid cities, struck dismay into Laches the general of the Athenians, who had a considerable fleet and had been sent to hinder the Thebans, and compelling him to sail away, made the cities the Thebans' own.
79.2. If, then, this man had lived a longer time, by common acknowledgement the Thebans would have acquired, in addition to the leadership by land, the rule of the sea; but since a little time later, in the battle about Mantinea, having won for his fatherland a most brilliant victory, he died heroically, immediately also the affairs of the Thebans died together with his death. But concerning these things we shall set forth the particulars accurately a little later.
79.3. At that time it seemed best to the Thebans to campaign against Orchomenus for some such causes as these. Certain of the exiles, wishing to change the constitution at Thebes into an aristocratic order, persuaded the horsemen of the Orchomenians, being three hundred, to share in the undertaking.
79.4. These, being accustomed to meet with the Thebans on an appointed day for the review under arms, agreed to make the attack on this. Many others sharing in the design and rushing forward, they met at the appointed time.
79.5. Those who had constituted the deed, repenting, made the attack known to the boeotarchs, betraying their fellow-conspirators, and through this service procured for themselves safety. The magistrates seizing the horsemen of the Orchomenians and bringing them into the assembly, the people voted to slaughter these and to enslave the Orchomenians and raze the city. For from ancient times the Thebans were ill disposed toward these, having paid tribute to the Minyae in the heroic times, and later having been freed by Heracles.
79.6. The Thebans, then, thinking they had an opportunity and having taken plausible pretexts for vengeance, campaigned against Orchomenus; mastering the city, they slew the men, and enslaved the children and women.
80.1. About the same times the Thessalians, being at war with Alexander the tyrant of Pherae, and being defeated in several battles and having lost many of their soldiers, sent envoys to the Thebans, asking them to help them and to send out Pelopidas as their general. For they knew this man, because of the arrest by Alexander, to be most ill disposed toward the ruler, and at the same time distinguished in valour and renowned for generalship's understanding.
80.2. The common assembly of the Boeotians being gathered, and the envoys having discoursed about the things of which they had instructions, the Boeotians granted everything to the Thessalians, and giving to Pelopidas up to seven thousand soldiers, ordered him to help quickly those who asked; but as Pelopidas was quickly going out with the force, it came to pass that the sun was eclipsed.
80.3. Many being suspicious of what had occurred, certain of the seers declared that because of the going out of the soldiers the sun of the city had been eclipsed. And through these words foretelling the death of Pelopidas, nonetheless Pelopidas broke camp for the campaign, being led by fate.
80.4. When he came to Thessaly and found Alexander having forestalled him in occupying the commanding positions and having more than twenty thousand soldiers, he encamped against the enemy, and taking on allies from the Thessalians joined battle with his opponents.
80.5. Alexander, because of the superiority of the places, having the advantage, Pelopidas, eager to decide the battle through his own valour, rushed against Alexander himself. The ruler withstanding with his chosen men, a fierce battle took place, in which Pelopidas, fighting bravely, strewed all the place about him with corpses; and at last, ending the danger and routing the enemy, he won the victory, but lost his own life, falling in with many wounds and giving up his life heroically.

80.6. Alexander, defeated in a second battle and crushed entirely, was compelled by agreement to give back to the Thessalians the cities he had subdued, and to deliver over the Magnetes and the Phthiotic Achaeans to the Boeotians, and for the rest, ruling Pherae alone, to be an ally to the Boeotians.
81.1. The Thebans, having carried off a renowned victory, said to all that they had been defeated because of the death of Pelopidas; for having lost a considerable man, they reasonably judged the victory to be less than the life of Pelopidas. For he had rendered many and great services to his fatherland, and contributed most to the increase of the Thebans. For in the return of the exiles, in which they recovered the Cadmeia, by common acknowledgement all assign to him the first place in the success. And this success came to be the cause of all the goods that occurred afterward.
81.2. In the battle about Tegyra Pelopidas alone of the boeotarchs conquered the Lacedaemonians, who were strongest of the Greeks, when, because of the magnitude of the victory, the Thebans first set up a trophy over the Lacedaemonians. In the battle at Leuctra he led the sacred band, with which, charging first against the Spartans, he became the author of the victory. In the campaigns against Lacedaemon he led seventy thousand, and by Sparta itself he set up a trophy over the Lacedaemonians, who all the time before had been unravaged.
81.3. Sending an embassy to the King of the Persians, in the common agreements he secured Messene privately, which, being desolate for three hundred years, the Thebans restored. At the end, fighting it out against Alexander, who had a force many times greater, he not only conspicuously conquered, but also had a death renowned for valour.
81.4. Toward the citizens he was so well disposed that from the return of the exiles to Thebes until his own death he continued boeotarch all the time, no other of the citizens having been deemed worthy of this honour. Pelopidas, then, having been deemed worthy of acceptance by all because of his own virtue, let him have also from us the praise through history.
81.5. About the same times Clearchus, being by descent from Heraclea on the Pontus, attempted a tyranny; mastering his undertaking, he emulated the way of life of Dionysius the tyrant of the Syracusans, and being tyrant of the Heracleotes ruled conspicuously twelve years.
81.6. At the same time as these things were being done, Timotheus the general of the Athenians, having an infantry and naval force, besieged and took Torone and Potidaea, and helped the Cyzicenes, who were being besieged.

82.1. This year having passed, at Athens the archon was Charicleides, and at Rome were appointed as consuls Lucius Aemilius Mamercus and Lucius Sextius Lateranus. In this year the Arcadians with the Pisatans had jointly held the contest of the Olympics, and were masters of the temple and the money in it. The Mantineans having taken into their private uses not a few of the dedications, those who had committed the lawlessness were eager to keep on the war against the Eleians, that they might not in peace give an account of what had been spent.
82.2. The other Arcadians wishing to conclude the peace, they stirred up factions against their countrymen. Two parties arising, it came to pass that the one had the Tegeates as leaders, the other the Mantineans.
82.3. The difference being greatly increased, they came to the decision by arms, and the Tegeates, sending an embassy to the Boeotians, persuaded them to help; the Boeotians, appointing Epaminondas general and giving him a considerable force, sent him out to help the Tegeates.
82.4. The Mantineans, struck with dismay at the force from Boeotia and the reputation of Epaminondas, sending envoys to the bitterest enemies of the Boeotians, the Athenians and Lacedaemonians, persuaded them to ally themselves. Both quickly sending strong forces, many and great contests arose in the Peloponnese.
82.5. Immediately, then, the Lacedaemonians, dwelling near, campaigned into Arcadia, while Epaminondas at this time, advancing with the force and being not far from Mantinea, learned from the natives that the Lacedaemonians in full force were ravaging the country of the Tegeates.
82.6. Supposing, then, that Sparta was empty of soldiers, he undertook to accomplish some great thing, but had fortune working against him. For he himself set out by night against Sparta, but the king of the Lacedaemonians, Agis, suspecting the quickness of wit of Epaminondas, prudently guessed the future, and sent certain Cretan day-runners, through whom, forestalling Epaminondas, he made known to those left in Sparta that the Boeotians would shortly come against Lacedaemon to plunder the city, and that he himself, as quickly as he could, would come with the force to help his fatherland. He bade those in Sparta guard the city, struck with dismay at nothing; for quickly he would appear and help.
83.1. The Cretans quickly doing what was ordered, unexpectedly the Lacedaemonians escaped the capture of their fatherland; for, the attack not being foretold, Epaminondas would have burst into Sparta unobserved. The device of both generals one might justly approve, but might consider the generalship of the Laconian the more prudent.
83.2. Nevertheless, Epaminondas, having stayed awake the whole night and hastily accomplished the distance of the road, at daybreak advanced against Sparta. Agesilaus, who had been left on guard, having a little before heard the particulars from the Cretans, immediately with much zeal took care of the city.
83.3. The eldest of the boys and the aged he sent up onto the roofs of the houses, and ordered them from these to defend against those who forced their way into the city, while he himself, arraying those in the prime of their ages, divided them into the difficult places and passes before the city, and blocking all the places able to receive a passage, awaited the onset of the enemy.
83.4. Epaminondas, dividing the soldiers into several parts and falling upon every place at the same time, when he saw the array of the Spartans, immediately knew that the deed had been betrayed; nevertheless, fighting against all in detail and being at a disadvantage in the difficult places, he came to close quarters.
83.5. Suffering and doing much, he did not desist from his ambition, until the army of the Lacedaemonians returned to Sparta; many coming to the aid of the besieged, and night coming on, he raised the siege.
84.1. Learning from the prisoners that the Mantineans in full force were present helping the Lacedaemonians, then, withdrawing a little from the city, he encamped; and ordering them to make their supper, leaving some of the horsemen, he ordered these until the morning watch to burn fires in the camp, while he himself, setting out with the force, hastened suddenly to fall upon those left in Mantinea.
84.2. On the next day, having accomplished a long road, he suddenly and unexpectedly dashed against the Mantineans, yet did not master his undertaking, although he had forethought everything by generalship, but, having fortune working against him, unexpectedly lost the victory. For just as he was drawing near the city, empty of men, there came to the other side of Mantinea the soldiers sent by the Athenians for the alliance, being six thousand, having as general Hegesileus, a man at that time praised among the citizens. This man, bringing the sufficient men into the city, drew up the rest of the force as if to be decided by battle.
84.3. Immediately also the Lacedaemonians and Mantineans appeared, and all prepared for the decision about the whole and sent for their allies from everywhere.
84.4. To the Mantineans, then, there came to help the Eleians and Lacedaemonians and Athenians and certain others, of whom the whole number was foot more than twenty thousand, and horse about two thousand; while with the Tegeates were allied the most and best of the Arcadians and Achaeans and Boeotians and Argives and certain others of the Peloponnesians and of the allies from outside; and all were gathered, foot above thirty thousand, and horse not fewer than three thousand.

85.1. Both sides eagerly going down to the contest about the whole, and the armies being drawn up, the seers on both sides, having sacrificed, declared that the victory was foreshown by the gods.
85.2. In the array the Mantineans with the other Arcadians held the right wing, having as comrades and fellow-fighters the Lacedaemonians, and continuous with these were the Eleians and Achaeans, and of the others the inferior held the middle array; the left wing the Athenians filled. The Thebans themselves were stationed on the left wing, having the Arcadians as comrades, and the right they gave to the Argives; the rest of the multitude filled the middle array, Euboeans and Locrians and Sicyonians, and besides these Messenians and Malians and Aenianians, and besides Thessalians and the rest of the allies. The horsemen on each of the wings both sides divided.
85.3. The armies being arrayed in this manner, when they were now near one another, the trumpets signalled the battle-cry, and the forces raised the war-shout and by the magnitude of the shout signalled the victory. And at first they constituted a cavalry battle on the wings, in which they surpassed one another in their rivalries.
85.4. For the horsemen of the Athenians, riding against those of the Thebans, were worsted, not so much by the excellences of the horses nor by their own courage nor by their experience in horsemanship—for in all these the cavalry of the Athenians was not inferior—but in the multitude and equipment of the light-armed and in the generalship's array they fell far behind their opponents. For they themselves had few javelin-throwers, while the Thebans had three times as many slingers and javelin-throwers sent from the regions about Thessaly.
85.5. These, having from childhood especially emulated the battle in these, were accustomed to make a great turn in battles because of their experience in them. Therefore the Athenians, being wounded by the light-armed and worn down by their opponents, all turned to flight.
85.6. Making their flight outside the wings, they corrected the defeat; for, in their withdrawal, they at once did not throw their own phalanx into disorder, and at the same time, falling in with Euboeans and certain mercenaries sent to seize the nearby hills, joining battle with them they slew them all.
85.7. The horsemen of the Thebans did not pursue the fleeing, but riding against the phalanx of those arrayed against them, were ambitious to outflank the infantry. A fierce battle taking place, and the Athenians being worn down and rushing to flight, the cavalry-commander of the Eleians, stationed in the rearguard, came to the aid of the fleeing, and laying low many of the Boeotians turned the battle the other way.
85.8. The horsemen of the Eleians, then, having in this manner appeared on the left wing, corrected the defeat that had occurred to the allies; while on the other wing, the horsemen dashing against one another, the battle remained for a brief time even, but after this, through the multitude and the valour of the Boeotian and Thessalian horsemen, those with the Mantineans were forced back, and losing many fled to their own phalanx.
86.1. The cavalry battle on both sides, then, had such an end; but the infantry forces, when they came to close quarters with the enemy, constituted great and wonderful contests. For never, when Greeks fought against Greeks, was so great a multitude of men arrayed, nor were there leaders more notable in their dignities, nor men more capable in displaying their bravery in dangers.
86.2. For those most able to fight on foot at the times in question, the Boeotians and Lacedaemonians, standing against one another in the array, first joined battle, making no sparing of life. And at first striking one another with their spears, and because of the density of the blows breaking most of them, they came to the contest of the sword.
86.3. Grappling with their bodies and working all manner of dispositions of wounds, they did not in their fury cease; and for a long time holding out in the terrors, because of the excess of the bravery on both sides, the battle took no turn; for each, despising to suffer anything terrible, and eager to do something brilliant, nobly received death for the sake of glory.
86.4. The battle being fierce for a long time and the danger taking no turn, Epaminondas, supposing that the victory required his own valour, resolved to decide the danger through himself. Immediately, then, taking up the best and with these locking shields together, he charged into the midst of the enemy; leading the way of his battalion, and first hurling his javelin, he struck the leader of the Lacedaemonians.
86.5. Immediately, as the others too came to close quarters, slaying some and striking dismay into others, he broke through the phalanx of the enemy.
